#6682. The Most Flattering Hairstyles for Women Over 50, From Bobs to Long Layers

The most flattering styles are less about age and more about shape, movement, and hair health.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The rules are relative when it comes to “age-appropriate hair.” No matter what decade you’re presently thriving in, the style you choose should make you feel good. That said, as hair texture, volume, and color change with age, some styles may feel and look better once you hit your 50s. The options are vast, but don’t think you have to go shorter as you mature or cover up sprouting grays. If anything, feel free to experiment. Worn short hair all your life? Try some extensions and waist-length waves. Or if you’ve had long hair for as long as you can remember, trim a few inches off into a happy medium lob. Experts share tips and ideas for choosing the best hairstyle if you’re over 50.

The most important thing is to choose for the hair you have now. “I tell my clients to think about things like fullness, movement, tone, and shape,” Elba Iris, John Frieda stylist and educator, tells ELLE. A good style, Elba adds, should make hair look healthy and as full as possible, have movement so it never looks stiff or set, and have shine with dimension. It’s also helpful to be realistic about your routine and consider how much daily effort and time you can commit to styling your hair.

Also, keep in mind that length is a personal choice. “One thing I really dislike is when women are told they need to cut their hair after a certain age,” says Rodger Azadganian, a hairstylist, salon owner, and founder of Äz Haircare. “I think that’s such an outdated idea. I care much more about the condition of the hair and whether the cut suits the person. If you love long hair, keep it long,” he encourages. Iris completely agrees, adding that shape, health, shine, and confidence are what make your hair look youthful.

Azadganian is a huge fan of a sharp bob, which he says always looks sophisticated. “I also love collarbone-length hair with a little movement around the face. And I think long, beautiful hair on a woman over 50 can be incredibly chic,” he adds.

Iris says the styles that consistently flatter his over-50 clients are those with softness around the face, deep angles, and layers if the hair is longer. Like Azadganian, Iris also says a collarbone-length lob with long soft layers is the most versatile. “It keeps length, gives movement, and [can be] styled in various ways,” says Iris. He adds that a textured bob, worn a little undone rather than perfectly smooth, is chic at any age and makes fine hair look thicker because the ends are blunt and full.

If you have or prefer short hair, Iris says a soft pixie with a longer, swept fringe is beautiful and lifts the whole face. “Face-framing layers or a soft curtain fringe are my secret weapon—they draw the eye up, soften everything, and grow out gracefully between appointments.”

Gray hair grows in with a different texture than you may be used to. It’s often wirier, drier, and more resistant to products and color, so styles may need more moisture and smoothing than before.

For those who dye their hair all one color and have started to, or are already fully gray, regrowth may pose an unflattering problem. “Solid color against graying regrowth creates a harsh line and can actually make thinning at the part more visible,” Iris cautions. Instead, both Iris and Azadganian recommend dimensional color over anything too flat or solid. Go for softer dimension—highlights, lowlights, or a blended “gray blending” approach. This technique diffuses the regrowth, adds the illusion of depth and fullness, and buys you more time between appointments.

If you’re embracing grey fully, love it. The key, though, according to Iris, is to keep it bright and conditioned. “Grey hair can yellow and look dull; a glossing treatment and the right purple shampoo, like John Frieda Violet Crush, keep it silver and striking instead of dusty. Color should work with your styling, never make it harder,” Iris recommends.

For fine hair, both Azadganian and Iris suggest keeping the ends blunt in order to make the hair look fuller. “A bob or lob with a strong perimeter makes hair look twice as dense, and I’d avoid heavy layering, which removes the fullness you can see. Fullness also has to be built at the styling,” Iris explains. He recommends the John Frieda Ultra Filler+ shampoo and conditioner for fine hair to plump each strand and to make hair look and feel thicker when styled. Use a thickening spray at the root before blow-drying for lasting lift.

For thick or coarse hair, go with longer layers to take out some weight and keep it from looking heavy and triangular. For curly and coily hair, Iris says shape is key. “A cut done on dry hair, in its natural state, with layers that let the curl sit where it lives, plus real moisture.”

Azadganian says a beautifully shaped curly bob is incredible. “I always want the haircut to work with the texture instead of forcing it into something else,” he notes.

Wavy hair looks best in a mid-length cut with soft layers that enhance the natural bend of the texture without heat styling. As for length, Iris says short hair loves texture and a little messiness. “Mid-length, chin to collarbone, is the sweet spot for most women because it’s long enough to feel feminine and short enough to stay full,” says Iris. Long hair after 50 absolutely works, but as both stylists noted, only if the hair is kept healthy and styled.

Azadganian says one of the biggest mistakes with hair over age 50 is getting stuck with the same hairstyle for decades. “You don’t need to change everything, but even updating your layers, fringe, or part can make such a difference. I love seeing women experiment with their hair at every age,” says Azadganian.

#6681. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6680. The Best Moisturizers for Softer, Smoother, More Resilient Skin After 40

As I write this, it’s two days before Thanksgiving in Chicago, and I’m tending to my prep work; to clarify, I don’t mean peeling potatoes. At 46, my skin gets ultra-dry this time of year, and getting ready for the holidays also means sourcing the best moisturizers for aging skin, lest I show up to seasonal celebrations looking dry and sallow—basically, anything but celebratory. So along with making a shopping list for the many side dishes in my future, I booked a Hydrating Facial at St. Regis Chicago’s spa—and maximized my time there by asking the team to fill me in on everything I need to know to stay moisturized at home.

“In your 40s, you may notice changes in your skin, including increased dryness, fine lines, loss of elasticity, and a decrease in overall radiance,” said Patty Aguilar, one of the spa’s esthetician. “At this stage, it's important to move beyond simply moisturizing and begin incorporating targeted ingredients that address your skin's changing needs while supporting its moisture barrier.”

A common mistake she sees older women making is focusing only on hydration while overlooking ingredients that can improve skin texture and tone. “I recommend looking for moisturizers that combine nourishing ingredients with gentle exfoliating or skin-renewing ingredients, such as lactic acid or fruit enzymes, when appropriate for your skin type,” she notes.

And though thick, cushiony creams can often feel the most luxurious on parched skin—particularly as winter approaches—Aguilar emphasizes that the right texture depends on individual skin types. A thicker moisturizer isn't necessarily more effective. What matters most is the formulation and whether the ingredients address your skin's specific needs. With that in mind, we've tapped skincare pros to share the best formulas for redness, dry skin, daytime, and more below. Winter is coming—stay moisturized out there!

“Our bodies produce less elastin and collagen as we get older,” Saedi acknowledges. “In fact, collagen production begins to slow as early as your mid-twenties. We start losing one percent of our collagen per year after that. By 40, collagen drops more dramatically.” As collagen and elastin decline, fine lines, wrinkles, and sagging becomes more noticeable in the skin. “Your face also loses volume as you age, and your skin will become thinner,” Saedi says.

But that’s not all. “Declining estrogen levels during perimenopause and menopause can also wreak havoc on your skin, contributing to dryness, dullness, thinning, and wrinkling in the skin,” Saedi says. “Lastly, sun damage accumulates over your lifetime and is one of the biggest causes of lines, wrinkles and unwanted pigmentation, also commonly referred to as sun spots.”

What is an ideal skincare regimen for mature skin?

According to Magovern, a morning skin care regime doesn’t have to start with face wash. “Don’t cleanse if skin feels dry or overprocessed, particularly if you did a good cleanse before bed,” she instructs. However, for mature skin that is “doing well and feeling strong,” she signs off on a gentle exfoliating cleanser that contains AHAs or PHAs.

Next up, a hydrating toner is “a great way to cleanse the skin without overwashing it,” she says, noting that “water can actually act as an irritant.” Follow the toning step with a serum that contains antioxidants, such as vitamin C, to protect and restore the skin. “You can also look for a serum with chemical exfoliators,” Magovern adds. “These can help remove some of those older surface skin cells and help the skin retain its ability to hold onto moisture and bring back the glow.” A rich moisturizer, followed by SPF, caps off the ideal morning regime.

In the evening, “gentle cleansers or oil cleansers are great choices for mature skin,” Magovern continues. “I prefer a gentle cleanser at night because subsequent steps tend to include more active products.” Exfoliation can also be part of a nighttime regime one to three times a week. “It may not be intuitive, but exfoliating the skin can actually help moisturize it because it removes the surface dead cells, which make it harder for the moisturizers to penetrate and work effectively,” says Magovern. “Exfoliators also help stimulate collagen production.” For mature skin, she recommends a chemical exfoliator with gentle AHAs like glycolic and lactic acids, and PHAs, like gluconolactone, which have moisturizing and antioxidant properties.

As a second-to-last step before bed, apply a treatment serum infused with active ingredients like retinol or peptides, which encourage cell turnover and cellular repair. “Sleep is the time when the cellular machinery is actively restoring and repairing, and it’s the perfect time to give the skin what it needs to help accomplish its nighttime work,” Magovern notes.

Lastly, apply a face moisturizer that helps the skin attract and retain moisture overnight. “Occluding the skin with a moisturizer also allows the active ingredients in the previous steps to penetrate deeper and perhaps work more effectively,” she says. “The moisturizing step is important for nourishing and hydrating the skin while you sleep.”

What ingredients work best in a moisturizer for aging skin?

“Hyaluronic acid and other humectants, like glycerin, are important to help attract and retain water in the skin,” says Ashley Magovern, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in Manhattan Beach, California, and medical advisor for Dermstore. “But, other ingredients are important for aging skin as well. Once you attract the water, it’s important to trap it and prevent water loss.” Occlusive agents like jojoba-seed oil or shea butter help lock moisture into the skin, while ceramides—lipids that help maintain and repair the skin barrier—“are critical in a moisturizer,” Magovern says.

Additionally, “moisturizers that include retinol—or using a retinoid or retinol serum in addition to your moisturizer—can help improve the appearance of elasticity, texture, pigmentation and wrinkles,” says Nazanin Saedi, MD, FAAD, a board-certified dermatologist in Philadelphia. “Caffeine helps plump the skin which can temporarily improve the appearance of sags and wrinkles. Other ingredients to look for would be ones that help stimulate and support the production of collagen: Peptides, vitamin C, niacinamide (vitamin B3), and growth factors.”

What kind of texture is ideal in a moisturizer for aging skin?

“As a rule of thumb, thicker consistencies are better at locking in moisture by literally creating a barrier on the skin’s outermost layer to prevent water from evaporating from the surface of the skin,” says Tony Nakhla, DO, medical director of OC Skin Institute in Orange County and founder of Eighth Day. “The more occlusive a product is, the more hydrating.”

However, hydration isn’t the only factor to consider. “The viscosity or thickness of a moisturizer is not as important to its efficacy as the active ingredient,” offers Stacey Tull, MD, MPH, board-certified dermatologic surgeon and owner of St. Charles County Dermatologic Surgery in Missouri. “Thicker moisturizers such as shea butter may not be as effective for some skin types as a thinner hyaluronic-acid-based product or an oil-based serum. Even at an older age, some people are still acne-prone and a heavy moisturizer would not be a good option for them. Likewise, someone with dry, fragile skin may benefit from a thicker, more emollient ointment or cream.”

What is the importance of a moisturizer for aging skin?

A moisturizer for mature skin is “absolutely vital,” says Rachel Nazarian, MD, FAAD, a board-certified dermatologist at Schweiger Dermatology in New York City. She explains that one one of the key clinical markers of aging skin is its inability to create and retain moisture naturally. “Loss of moisture can make skin look more flaccid, less youthful, and dull,” Nazarian says.

Furthermore, “dry skin leads to inflammation, even if you can’t see it,” says Magovern. “Inflamed skin will not tolerate all the active skin care products that we all want to use, so it’s imperative to keep that barrier strong. Furthermore, inflamed skin will trigger your skin problems like eczema, seborrheic dermatitis, and rosacea, so it’s important to keep the skin moisturized. Hydrated skin also just looks smoother, younger and brighter.” In short, she says: “There are so many reasons to moisturize.”

Ingredients to Look for in a Moisturizer for Aging Skin

The best moisturizers for aging skin contain key ingredients that tackle everything from dryness to sagging and dark under-eye circles. Below, top dermatologists and a plastic and reconstructive surgeon break down the best ingredients to look for when scouting out a moisturizer that can almost appear to rewind time—or at the very least, diminish the appearance of wrinkles.

What to Consider in a Moisturizer for Aging Skin

The best moisturizers for aging skin have just the right balance of rich, hydrating texture, anti-aging ingredients, and benefits tailored to one’s individual skin type. How to choose the right moisturizer for you? “Depending on your skin type—whether you are dry, oily, normal or combination—you may opt for different ingredients and formulation types, such as gel, lotion, or cream,” says Libby.

On another ingredient note, Libby says that it’s wise for those with sensitive skin to avoid potential irritants such alcohol, fragrances, and essential oils.

#6679. Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She says more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

#6677. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

#6676. Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”

#6675. Photographer Franco Rubartelli Shares the Stories Behind Some of Vogue’s Most Famous ‘60s Shoots

Franco Rubartelli and Veruschka on location in Brazil.

Editor’s Note: Veruschka, the most super of ’60s models, has died. Her love affair with Franco Rubartelli played out in the pages of Vogue. In memoriam we are revisiting this interview with the photographer who wrote of Veruschka on Instagram: “She wasn’t just a great model. She was an elegant woman, sensitive, brave, with a beauty that did not stay in the camera, it would get into the soul of whoever watched her. She had a way of being in the world that you don't learn; you take in. People like Veruschka don’t go away at all. They stay in a picture, in a perfume, in a song, in a way of smiling.”

The 1960s were a heady time of change and youth and fantasy. This was also the case in Vogue, then led by Diana Vreeland, who brought her own taste for historicism and exoticism to its pages. “For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible,” says Franco Rubartelli, who, between 1964 and 1970, created some of the most memorable photographs ever published in the magazine. Presented in multipage spreads and taken in far-flung locales, these now-iconic images are exemplars of an elevated and romanticized hippie ethos. On a personal level, they documented one of fashion’s great love affairs.

Rubartelli, born in Florence, is a self-taught photographer who had planned to follow his father into the Italian Navy. He was pursuing his back-up plan, diplomacy, when Cupid arranged a collision that eventually steered him toward fashion. Enrolled at Cambridge to study English, Rubartelli recounts, he went to a pub to meet a blind date—who stood him up. As he rose to leave, he collided with a waitress carrying a tray of beer, which doused him. The tray bearer in question was a Swiss beauty named Françoise Schluter, earning pocket money at the pub while studying languages at the university. It was amore, and soon Rubartelli and Schluter were a couple. They married and lived in Rome with their son, Luigi. Tall, lithe, and blonde, Schluter was discovered on the streets there and started modeling. Her career transformed Rubartelli, by his own admission, into the archetypal jealous husband.

With her “scrubbed good looks,” Françoise Rubartelli models “American Sports Clothes in Italy.”

One night, after having mysteriously found a camera in their apartment, Rubartelli asked Schluter to pose for him on a beach. With no stylist, hair, or makeup—nor much knowledge of how the camera worked—he took pictures of the wife he feared he was losing, pictures that were infused with longing, youth, and freedom—qualities rarely expressed in the formal fashion photographs of the time. Having asked Schluter what the most important magazine was, Rubartelli got together some money to develop the film and secretly sent the results to Vogue.

Much to Rubartelli’s surprise, he received a positive reply from New York in the form of a telegram, signed Diana Vreeland, then Vogue’s editor in chief, that read: “Beautiful model, beautiful pictures, will get in touch with you.” Soon, the photographer and his model wife were working with Consuelo Crespi, the magazine’s editor in Rome; their first story appeared in the August 1964 issue. As Rubartelli and Schluter were racking up credits and becoming known as a couple, though, their love story was unraveling. “We spent too much time together as photographer and model, and not enough as man and woman,” Rubartelli explains via email. Their final rupture (circa 1965) left Rubartelli “without work, without my wife, without my model, without my son.”

Another no-show launched the second chapter of Rubartelli’s Vogue career. Having received a call about an advertising job, the young photographer went to meet the client at the Parco dei Principi Grand Hotel in Rome. He remembers that as he waited, and waited some more, “a tall, skinny woman in a black cloak and long knee-high boots walked past and caught my attention.” Rubartelli asked the concierge who she was and was told she was a German model, at which point he called his mother and asked her to pose as his secretary and invite this alluring Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort, aka Veruschka, to stop by his studio with her portfolio. “At this point,” Rubartelli explains, “my name was known through my work for Vogue. Veruschka stopped by in the early afternoon and we talked until the evening. I invited her to dinner at a restaurant. We spoke about Françoise, and she told me about her family. We shared our problems and stayed talking like two parrots until an innkeeper told us it was closing time. It was very late. We spent the rest of that night and every successive night together for nearly nine years. It was love at first sight.”

Theirs was a creative relationship that flourished in print and in life and took the pair around the globe. Recently Rubartelli, now living in Venezuela, has started to use Instagram as a biographical platform. Having spent endless hours poring over ’60s Vogues and becoming especially curious about Rubartelli and his models, his Instagram diary left me spellbound and eager to know more. I reached out to the ebullient Rubartelli, who openly and graciously agreed to share some personal stories with me.

“You know something?” Rubartelli recently wrote, “I think that I have never been a photographer. I was simply a man who loved the two most important women of his life through his camera. I remember how beautiful my pictures came out when I was in love with Françoise or Veruschka, and when our stories ended, when there was no more feeling between us, I could stay for hours and hours in front of them without doing one good picture.” Rubartelli does himself a disservice. The Vogue archive provides evidence that he very much has a feeling for the form.

Here, the stories behind some of his best-known Vogue assignments.

“[After meeting and falling in love], we decided to take some photos together. Veruschka was very tall—her size was not commercial for the fashionable photos at that time—so we got to thinking about doing something different, and we came up with the idea of body painting. No one had been doing this.”

“We bought colorful makeup, feathers, and paillettes and decided, on our own dime, to go to the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas. There we painted Veruschka’s naked body.”

“During the time we shared together, I noticed that Veruschka carried with her inferiority complexes from her childhood. It sometimes felt as if she were not happy in her body, that her personality wanted to evade its physical dimension to become other beings. She found in makeup the possibility of escaping and transforming into other things: a butterfly that could fly, a panther or a tiger to run in the jungle, a mermaid to sink into the sea.”

“We often went to Veruschka’s mother’s house in Petersrkirchen, near Munich. She was a very open-minded lady and very proud of Vera. She lived in a big house with many rooms. When we visited, our rooms were under the roof on the second floor. They were very big and all built in wood.”

“Veruschka’s mother lived a drama with all her daughters during the Second World War. Her husband, [Heinrich Graf von Lehndorff-Steinort], participated in the plot to kill Hitler in his bunker. It was not successful, and he was executed. [According to Der Spiegel, Vera’s mother, Gottliebe, was first put in prison and then placed in a working camp with her newborn child. Her older daughters were moved, with other children of the resistance, to a nursing home and renamed.] Reunited after the war, they moved from one place to another and were very poor. When I met Vera’s mother, she had a boyfriend living with her. He was a crazy musician playing very heavy and noisy music. Her mother loved him and his music. In winter, the place was very beautiful. It was near a forest, and the fog made a great atmosphere.” From left: Countesses Catharina and Vera (known as Veruschka) von Lehndorff, Frau Marie Eleonora von Haeften, and Baroness Gabriela von Plotho.

“The Queen Christina assignment came about while we were watching the movie [about her] starring the tremendous Greta Garbo. Before the film was over, Veruschka and I simultaneously had the idea to propose the look of the queen to Diana Vreeland. Enthusiastic, we asked for an appointment with her and got one for the following week. This meant that we had to work day and night without sleeping to have the project ready with sketches. If we weren’t on time, we’d have to wait a long time to see her. We were always a little nervous about what Mrs. Vreeland’s reaction would be. She was a very straight woman; if she liked an idea, she would accept it right away; if she didn’t like it, we understood immediately that the project did not work for Vogue. She was very fond of us, but didn’t care about our reaction if she did not like the idea.”

“Mrs. Vreeland’s mysterious office [was infused] with the smell of her candle. How she walked, how she moved her hands with her long, expressive fingers, was very exotic. She created a magical atmosphere in her office, which had black walls full of photographs and furniture upholstered in an intense red fabric, mixed with leopard skins. In this dim environment you almost didn’t see Vreeland, who dressed all in black and red and almost matched the decor. ‘How are you, Mrs. Vreeland?’ asked Veruschka. We explained all the details and she listened in silence. It was a silence that was scary. Finally, when we finished, she got to her feet and congratulated us, saying: ‘This is so fabulous; let’s do it!’”

“Mrs. Vreeland loved the Queen Christina idea and ordered dresses to be made for Veruschka. We headed to Austria, where we made Innsbruck our base. For 10 days we looked for locations. It wasn’t easy to find a castle.”

“Mrs. Vreeland almost never rejected an idea: Queen Christina, Libya, Texas, Australia, Brazil . . . . For Vreeland, everything impossible was possible, and she didn’t put limits on our creativity. This was very stimulating for us, because every project we proposed was more daring. I remember one time she called us by surprise and asked us to go to Rio de Janeiro to photograph some dresses during Carnival. She showed us the clothes and explained her idea to us. ‘Franco,’ she said, ‘I do not want to see the Carnival; I want you to work in a studio with the windows opened. Franco,’ she continued, ‘I want, I want . . . pissst.’ She made a buzzing noise with her mouth closed. ‘I want you to shoot like that. Do you understand what I mean?’ I did not. It was impossible to understand what she meant with that sound.”

“I think Mrs. Vreeland was very original. Having such an important position in the world of fashion in those years, she directed taste toward the different, the eccentric. She understood things immediately, and if she liked an idea, she approved it on the spot. She had very precise ideas about colors; for example, she loved red and dressed in it and decorated her apartment in it. Apart from her strong and precise ideas of color, one could never be sure about her decisions until the last moment. Once she liked an idea and authorized it, she approved the costs of the productions. There was never an intention to reduce the result by making any kind of economy.”

“I can assure you, without a doubt, that Veruschka, myself, and Giorgio di Sant’Angelo [a textile designer turned stylist and designer] were a creative team for a long period. We met together to develop themes, and if we had a trip that we liked, we gave ourselves to the story until we fully developed it. Veruschka and I really enjoyed going to Giorgio’s house. We spent many hours there thinking, drawing ideas, doing tests. Then, back in the city, we visited museums, bought books to study, saw films, all to perfect our ideas and to make sure of the look that we wanted to create.”

“Giorgio [above right] was unlike anyone else; his creativity was superior. He had been born in Florence, Italy, but had spent so much time outside of the country that he had forgotten the language a little; when he spoke, it was a funny [argot]. He was an original and very imaginative designer. Giorgio was an excellent companion also in private life. He shared with his friends the joyful moments as well as the anxious ones and tried to creative a positive atmosphere. His style tended toward the exotic. His only defect was that he smoked too much; he was never without a cigarette in his hand. He was an artist in creating jewelry, and he himself was upholstered in necklaces of all kinds.”

“Giorgio loved colors and their mixture. I studied him as we prepared for our journey to the Painted Desert. In order to decide what fabrics to bring with us, he came to the studio with many samples of all colors. In front of a mirror he tested the various combinations by cutting and mixing the different pieces with incredible taste and perfection. It was fun to see him. He looked like a scarecrow all covered in pieces of cloth. For the final test shots on Veruschka, he invented the gypsy look by cutting all sorts of fabrics and wrapping them around the body.”

“When we decided to work in the desert of Libya, we visited many stores looking for fabrics suitable for all the drapings that would be made on location. They weren’t sewn dresses, but draped on the body. We were creating a look, an atmosphere—nothing more. We went to Diana Vreeland to sell her an atmosphere, and she accepted it and gave us carte blanche. Of course, we had our sketches, but sometimes we were moved by feelings, or so inspired by the atmosphere, that we were forced to change things.”

“Every morning in one location or another, Veruschka, almost naked, was standing for many hours as Giorgio draped on her body. These preparations were incredible. In the sand around us there were meters of fabric that Giorgio cut and adapted to her body. We had a long mirror that Veruschka could see herself in. Although we always started early in the morning, before dawn, these preparations lasted many hours, and I worried and complained because the light became too strong. We couldn’t work later than 10:00 a.m.; we could start again after 4:00 p.m. when the desert light turned gold.”

“I remember that when we traveled, Giorgio spent a lot of time researching, trying to find original clothes typical of each place we were visiting. Before our shoot in Ghadames, he went to visit the small souk of the town, where he discovered two small warehouses full of typical desert fabrics and bought many of them. As he did not have much money, he made a deal with the store owner, agreeing to swap the fabrics he had brought for the ones in the souk, so Giorgio returned to New York with stupendous finds.”

“Giorgio came to the desert shoot every day with two or three suitcases full of fabrics that he modeled on Veruschka’s body according to his state of mind. He spread the fabrics out on the ground so he could have a panoramic view of them all. One day a strong breeze blew in all of a sudden and the fabrics began to fly away. It was amusing to see Giorgio run after them in the dunes, and suddenly stumble and fall. Once we were approached by a little girl from Ghadames. She was very cute and watched us curiously. After a while she grabbed a piece of fabric and put it on her head, simulating what Giorgio was doing with Veruschka. We asked her not to touch and to go away, but Giorgio stopped what he was doing with Veruschka and draped some fabric on her, then he cut the cloth and let the girl run away with ‘a custom Giorgio di Sant’Angelo.’”

#6674. How Did This 14-Year-Old Get Sam Bankman-Fried on the Phone?

Journalists who’ve been anxious about losing their jobs to artificial intelligence would be wise to focus on a different, altogether less menacing but equally impressive threat: 14-year-old Eli Goldfine, the shoestring podcaster from Westchester County who last week conducted a 90-minute interview with Sam Bankman-Fried, who’s currently serving a 25-year sentence in federal prison for orchestrating a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency grift.

So how, exactly, does this precocious ninth grader with braces—and not a reporter from one of the scores of legacy publications who’d surely be gunning for access to the disgraced cryptocurrency king—score an interview so coveted? “I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam’s account,” Goldfine, who hosts a podcast about prediction markets called The Supercycle, told me earlier this week. “I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case.”

Goldfine’s classmates are impressed, too, even though he’s been on the receiving end of some gentle ribbing about his on-air ad reads. But can any of them say they got Bankman-Fried to speculate on the likelihood that AI will bring about the extinction of the human race? ("Less than 50%, more than 10%," by the way). Before school’s out for Thanksgiving break, Goldfine joined GQ to talk about his media diet, dream interview subject, and the mechanics of interviewing a man behind bars.

Eli Goldfine: Wait, just to step back here. Are you printing what I'm going to say, or is this just for you to know? It's not a video on the site, right?

Okay. So my podcast is primarily about prediction markets and other broader markets. And I got into that during the 2024 election. My dad showed me Polymarket and I thought, "Wow, this is really cool. It's people staking money on different sides of an outcome. And when you put all that price signal together, it converges on a really accurate probability of a given event happening. How could I investigate this more?" So I learned more about it and I started trading on a fake-money version of Polymarket.

It's called Manifold Markets. And what's cool about that one is, anyone can create their own question rather than the platform deciding. And anyway, I got really into it and then I was like, “I'll write a couple articles about this because I have some ideas.” And then I started doing interviews and it all kind of came out from that.

I think sports betting, like FanDuel and DraftKings—this stuff obviously serves very little utility because it's just the company offering these bets to the gamblers and there's no really accurate price signal coming out of that. So does that serve such an important function? Probably not. And it's fair to say the same about prediction markets on sports. Does anyone really need to know the outcome of a sports game that badly? I mean, probably not. I don't have anything against it per se, because people spend money for entertainment on other things. I mean, this is another way to spend your money. But it's not as valuable as prediction markets in some other categories. Right?

I mean, I think I've just always had a motivation to learn more about what I'm interested in. So when I start learning about something, I just get it all in my head and then I can talk about it pretty competently, I guess. I wouldn't consider myself to have natural interviewing skill. I just think I know a lot about the things that I'm interested in.

So for news, mostly Bloomberg. For social media, mostly Twitter. And then I also read articles on Substack.

So I think I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam's Twitter account. And they said, "I run this Twitter account now, but I think you have some smart ideas about Sam. Would you be interested in taking over the Twitter account?" And I was like, "Oh, yeah, that could be fun." And my dad was like, "No, you can't do that. I don't want to get sued or anything." So we ended up talking to Sam's parents about it, and they were disappointed that I wouldn't be able to take over the Twitter account. But as an alternative, they proposed, "You should just interview Sam for your podcast." So I just thought, "Wow, that's a great idea. Let's do that."

Oh, I don't know. I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case, which we actually didn't cover very much during our podcast together, since it's already been widely covered. But, yeah, I think I just had learned a lot about the case and they were like, "Well, maybe we want someone who knows a lot about the case to be able to take over his Twitter."

I don't know. I might want to skip that one for legal reasons.

I mean, I've watched so many of his other interviews, both when he was behind bars and before that, and I feel like he talks the same way to everyone. So I'm 14, you would expect maybe the average person is going to talk a little bit differently to a 14-year-old interviewer. But for him, I think it was pretty much the same, which is kind of what I expected. He's very consistent when he's talking to different people.

So when he picked up and was like, "Hi, it's Sam," I was like, "Wow, I've heard him say this in so many other interviews, but he's talking to me. That's crazy." He also called 15 minutes before the scheduled time, so I was panicking a little bit trying to get all my questions in order and deciding what order I was going to ask them in. I mean, it was pretty intense. And also, it was split up over two days in three hour windows during each day, since he can only call for 15 minutes at a time. So that was a little bit stressful.

I mean, it's mostly what I expected. He just hadn't really gone on the record about it specifically, which is why I wanted to ask him. I think his views are pretty common. He's a part of the effective altruism community. So I wasn't so surprised when he said he thought there was a 25% chance of AI destroying humanity. Obviously, if it's the average person, that might seem a little surprising. But knowing him, I wasn't very surprised.

I think there's going to be a lot of benefit in the short term, especially when we're seeing the rate of technological progress. Just in the past few months, AI has solved multiple millennium problems, which has been a huge deal. So I think there's definitely potential of AI curing diseases over the short term. But in the long term, you have to consider that there's a few examples of less intelligent things controlling more intelligent things, and that's kind of the whole point that the doomers are trying to make. Just that, when humans were smarter than the next smartest animal, we’re the ones who dominated, right?

At the end of the interview, I asked him what I call the coin flip question. "Would you take a 51-49 bet of doubling the world or destroying it?" And mostly people just think it's funny. Some responses that have been less good were people focusing on the ad read I did during the episode and mistaking it for a sportsbook, even though it's actually a free-to-play forecasting competition. Ninth grade. And I live in Westchester County, New York.

#6673. “The Most Beautitul Woman in the World…”: Richard Avedon’s Ode to Veruschka in 1972

TWO SPECTACULARS Veruschka, one of the great wonders of our time, here, with another: the Great Chrysanthemum Diamond, a remarkable 104.15 carats, made even more so by its color—a deep golden brown with flashes of orange, green, blue, and scarlet.

Editor’s note: Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort—the model best known as Veruschka—died on November 24, according to a report in the German tabloid Bild. She was 87.

Veruschka was a frequent presence in the pages of Vogue throughout the 1960s and ’70s, appearing on the cover at least a dozen times and posing for photographers including Irving Penn, Franco Rubartelli, Horst P. Horst, Bert Stern, and Richard Avedon, who considered her a muse.

Indeed, in 1972, Avedon penned a tribute to Veruschka, the ur-supermodel, for Vogue’s May issue. We have reprinted that text—and the original captions, which breathlessly celebrate Veruschka’s famously lithe figure—here.

Veruschka is the most beautiful woman in the whole world. There’s just nobody like her. If she’s beautiful, she’s beautiful alone. There are imitations of Sophia Loren, only not as good, and a new Garbo is discovered every decade, but there is and will always be only one Veruschka. Beauty isolates the person who owns it and isolation makes demands on the imagination. Veruschka’s bones, her body, her extraordinary length have compelled her to invent her own person. There’s just no one she could imitate.

There’s never enough of her. Each encounter is unfulfilled and unforgettable. It has nothing to do with ordinary life. The last time I photographed her she said, “Goodbye for now,” and then she didn’t come back for five years. When she finally walked in, I felt as if we’d both been waiting every day of those years between. I couldn’t disappoint her.

I love looking at her through the dressing-room door. It’s usually pretty crowded in there and she sits at the dressing table with her tea and honey, naked, oblivious to hairdressers, fashion editors and assistants, making up her face with a Japanese paintbrush. She has the concentration of a child playing some totally private, wordless game alone as she places the shadows where she wants them and the highlights where she thinks they belong.

She chooses words very carefully. She talks about her skin as if it has a mind of its own. It can be tired when she’s not. She speaks of her hair as a head of independent hairs and calls them “my hairs,” even the baby ones at the back of her neck. And that’s not a grammatical error. It has to do with consideration.

VITALITY…VERUSCHKA EXPLODES WITH IT Flying mane, flashing smile, Veruschka lighting up the day in her own bright white pants suit, black-and-white shirt and boots. … She is, quite simply, an extraordinary natural beauty. Like other great beauties, she insists upon a régime aimed at keeping those looks, that fantastic energy at their peak... part of Veruschka’s program, next pages.... Suit and shirt, by Antony Arland; boots, by Nazareno Gabrielli. All, designed especially for Veruschka. Scarf by Halston.

She’ll cover her breasts in front of some and not in front of others. That selectivity has implications of intimacy and trust. It’s a commitment. She’s sensitive to the fact that she’s undressed and you’re there and it’s full of nuances which she will neither deny nor resolve. They become resolved in the work.

I love talking with her because of that voice. There’s none like it, deep, unimaginably soft, and, for a romantic girl, remarkably unsentimental, which gives romance its real power. She knows the value of a quiet, two-hour conversation before going on the set. The time is never wasted. Her skin is like litmus paper for her feelings. She’s all made up and ready and, as we sit together, her skin gets very warm in color and then, suddenly, it drains. The second the color leaves her face, I know she’s ready to work.

Veruschka is the only woman I permit to look at herself in the mirror while I’m photographing her. The mirror makes most women aware of their weaknesses and, in trying to correct them, they come up with evasions, hiding arms that seem too thin or hips that seem too wide. Veruschka knows that it is what’s peculiar to her that’s beautiful and she works to bring it forward. It’s wonderful to see her searching for and emphasizing her irregularities.

EXERCISE...VERUSCHKA’S SARAN SAUNA, HER MIRACLE TUBE-STRETCH Clinging coats of Dow’s Saran Wrap around her body, Veruschka, opposite, wrapped for exercise. Within half an hour, this individual sauna has forced the body to shed more tissue-locked water than a real sauna could have done. Same technique can be used on any problem area—upper arms, thighs, waist—of any body, even one in such enviable shape as Veruschka’s. This was hit upon by top-notch Manhattan gymnast and exercise director Venizelos Antoniadis... Left, the two-way-stretch exercise tube designed by Giorgio di Sant’ Angelo in the marvelous Patternskin fabric that he developed from Du Pont’s Antron nylon and Lycra for United Elastic. The dress has its own Dr. Denton-like feel, and stretching in it is “like working against a wall”—but when not stretching as here, “it falls beautifully, very cloudy and soft,” says Giorgio.

There are times during a sitting when she turns to look at me or at the camera and, without so much as lifting an eyebrow or curving her mouth, smiles, challenges. It’s like the opposite of the Dylan song, “I’ll let you in my dream if you’ll let me in yours.” That seems to be what most people need. But not Veruschka. She’ll let you look into her dream but she wouldn’t fit in yours.

There’s a profoundly moving moment at the end of every sitting with Veruschka when I say, “I think I’ve got it.” She looks at me with a startled expression that comes very quickly across her face. I once asked her what she hopes for from a sitting, why she does it, and she said, “When I was a child I loved things because they were beautiful, but that isn’t enough. I want to do something with it. You make photographs. I would like to do it with my own body. I’m fascinated to see myself reproduced again, that there is no end of looking always a little bit different. And this is like a wine or a drug or something. You always have to have another one.” Ending the sitting, which is something only I can do, is like an interruption. I feel as if I’m taking her away from work that, for her, will always be unfinished.

YOGA...FOR SERENITY OF MIND, FOR LIMBERNESS OF BODY Veruschka puts her incredible body through the slow motions of advanced yoga under the guidance of the renowned Swami Satchidananda. Top left, the Ardha Matsyendrasana or half spiral twist. Top right, a variation of the Supta Vojrasana, or bent pelvic pose. Bottom right, the Sarvangasana, or shoulder stand, and, most strikingly, above, the Yoga Nidrasana, or yogic sleep pose. Her diaper-wrap yoga suit, in cashmere-like Nomelle yarn of Orlon, by Giorgio di Sant’ Angelo.

It’s impossible to be beautiful without being moving and impossible to be moving without a sense of irony. Veruschka makes me laugh a lot. She makes everybody laugh. At her most remarkable, when everything is perfect and the light is on her and we are all frozen by what she has accomplished, she sinks a little deeper into her knees, looks at my assistant holding the light, and says, “He makes good lightning, no?”

It is both deliberate and a little hesitant. She keeps you guessing about how much she really knows. She seems to hover, waiting for the laughter. It’s the subtlest kind of demand. It’s not just that she’s said something funny. She’s made you want to laugh for her.

She turns words around. She turns everything around. Her presence in a room calls it all into question, what you thought you knew, what you were sure of. Nothing looks the same as it did before she got there. Tall girls become short girls. Brown walls go golden. Being beautiful in her way demands something and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever.

THIS IS WHAT IT’S ALL ABOUT...TO LOOK LIKE THIS After all the exercise, the polishing, the yoga—the knockout punch of Veruschka at night. The relaxed, alive beauty of radiant skin and gleaming hair; the end that more than justifies the means. The bias black silk crêpe dress, left, the sexiest bared black dress in a season of sexy, bare, black dresses. By Stavropoulos, of Peter Griffin silk. Black coil bracelet by Paul Iwao. Ring, of exquisitely matched pieces of marble cone shell encased in gold, by Marguerite Stix for Cartier, Veruschka’s coif by Ara Gallant.

The sugar plums:Here, we’ve used walnuts, prunes, apricots, and dates, but feel free to switch it up as you like! #6670. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6669. With ‘A Kidman Carol,’ Marla Mindelle, Josh Sharp, and Kevin Zak Fête Australia’s Two Greatest Exports

It started, as things often do for Kevin Zak, as an idea for a meme.

The playwright behind last year’s Ginger Twinsies, a Millennial satire of The Parent Trap, is more widely known for his presence on social media, where his pop culture memes sit right at the corner of Extremely Online and Incredibly Gay. (This likely had something to do, he admits, with growing up with two gay brothers and a father who would decorate their front door with a giant Academy Award cutout on Oscars night.)

A Kidman Carol, his latest play, stemmed from his idea for a spin on the Dickens classic in which Cate Blanchett is visited by Nicole Kidman in order to learn the true meaning of awards season. When a friend who runs the Alleyway Theatre in Buffalo, New York, offered a few nights to workshop anything he wanted in 2024, Zak knew just the holiday program he wanted to see.

Enter Marla Mindelle and Josh Sharp, who now play Kidman and Blanchett in the show’s off-Broadway premiere. As Mindelle puts it, “The world of theater is so small, off-Broadway even smaller, and alt queer comedy is literally a basement limited to about 10 people, and we are three out of those 10.” She has a point: Mindelle’s massively popular Titanique and Sharp’s A24-backed film Dicks: The Musical both started at (literally) underground comedy clubs.

When Zak asked them if they’d like to participate in a workshop presentation that took place last winter, Mindelle says she and Sharp texted on the side: “I’ll do it if you do it. It’s five performances. What can go wrong?”

Sharp and Richard Perez in A Kidman Carol.

“And what can go wrong is a full six-week run at the off-Broadway mall,” Sharp quips, referencing the curious, five-theater layout of New World Stages.

Just in time for the holidays, and with awards season just around the corner, Vogue caught up with the comedy trio to discuss Kidman and Blanchett’s unending star power.

Vogue: Was there ever a question as to which stars you wanted to feature in the show?

Kevin Zak: It was always centered around them.

Josh Sharp: They sort of exemplify this distinction really well, where Cate is more of a “pure actress” who’s like, “Why do I have to make TikToks? I want to act.” And, in the show, we get into how Nicole has leveraged some of that power to be like, “Because I’m a celebrity, I can make all this stuff.” I think because Cate is a person that people know less [about]—you don’t really have a Cate Blanchett impression—she feels a little more like everywoman, and it means we can bend her into being Scrooge. She’s mostly known for her intensity, so she can become a good stand-in for a curmudgeon who wishes the state of the world were different, and Nicole can agree but be a bit more hopeful about it. How do they change each other?

Zak: Besides being all lesbians that have mental breakdowns, Cate’s characters all have the energy of, The world is against me, everyone is trying to get me, like in Tár or Carol or Notes on a Scandal. That feels like a good engine for her throughout the show: As curmudgeonly as she comes across, she’s trying to open your eyes to what the hell is going on, and is anyone going to do anything about it?

This is a very earnestly pro-awards show play. What was the last shockingly good Oscar win?

Marla Mindelle: What if I said Adrian Brody’s second Oscar?

Sharp: What if I said Green Book? There’s gotta be one past this, but my gut goes with Moonlight winning best picture. That was such an affirming culture-stopper to me, where I was like, Thank God we’re allowing movies like that, with zero dollars, to actually win.

Zak: Minari, when Youn Yuh-jung won [for best supporting actress]. Brad Pitt was a producer of the movie and she scolded him for never coming to set during her acceptance speech.

Marla, what have you discovered in your Nicole deep dive?

Mindelle: I rewatched To Die For, which I think actually might be my favorite Nicole Kidman film, even over Moulin Rouge!, which I can’t believe I’m saying because Moulin Rouge! was also my sexual awakening. Compared to Cate, I feel like Nicole has 10% more camp. Nicole knows what she is serving and has a little wink about it, like “I know I’m so beautiful and so talented,” where Cate is: “Yes, and I’m also all about the work.”

Zak: What makes them different in their performances, at least for me, is that Nicole’s characters get hurt and Cate’s characters get mad. In Big Little Lies, you see this woman in this horrible relationship get hurt, even in her therapy sessions. Even when her therapist is so bluntly truthful with her, all she can really say is, “I think you’re way out of line,” which is a line in our show. Cate is on the defensive. I feel that hurt is disguised with rage, a lot of the time. But that’s what really draws me to them, that core emotional difference. And they’ve never done a movie together, which is so crazy.

When did you each realize Nicole was a star?

Zak: Definitely Dr. Chase Meridian in Batman Forever.

Mindelle: I remember her having sex in To Die For. That was a pivotal moment where I was like, Oh my God, what is this feeling so sudden and new inside my body? I re-watched it recently and it really is one of the greatest movies ever. She is phenomenal.

Zak: That makes sense. [It’s] why you play her so horny.

Mindelle: It’s not even horny. I just feel like she’s always, like, loose and up for anything.

Mindelle: If you offered her poppers at The Eagle, she’d be like, “Why not?” She’ll do it.

Sharp: I’ve loved The Talented Mr. Ripley since I was young, but I really think Tár is one of the greatest films of the decade. I saw it four times in theaters. I heard people go, “Isn’t it sort of so long and slow and boring?” I’m like, Absolutely, let’s go!

Zak: Notes on a Scandal. I remember going to see it for Judi Dench and then being served Cate Blanchett having a mental breakdown in that press sequence, with her black eyeliner running as she’s just moan-screaming to be left alone. I finally saw myself onscreen.

In writing and preparing for this, were you trying to get into what these women are actually like, or was it all based on their public perception?

Zak: There is a combo of both. Cate, especially, her version of Scrooge is not someone we disagree with, like we do in A Christmas Carol. She makes solid points about the state of, not only the industry, but the planet. She’s been very vocal about her opinions. Her foundation is an anti-AI foundation and, on Las Culturistas, she spoke about how much award season has gotten overblown and how it should be a private event, if we’re going to do it at all. And then, of course, there’s her tirade on leaf blowers and how much she hates them. And then Nicole is truly up for anything, but she also uplifts people. She’s spoken a lot about how she uses her name to uplift young female screenwriters, young female directors, and putting her name on projects so that they get greenlit.

Marla, how’d you develop your insanely good Kidman impression?

Mindelle: The great thing about doing a role like this—a minimal, meaty role like this—is that it’s made me watch a lot of old Nicole Kidman movies. I feel like a kid again because I’m watching all these incredibly nostalgic movies from the ’80s, ’90s, and realizing her body of work is absolutely incredible. And whatever she has become now is almost this camp amalgamation of the past 30 to 40 years of her work. We’re just living in her timeline.

Zak: It feels like there’s never been a dip for Nicole, in terms of movie stardom. She’s only continued to rise in likability, popularity, talent, star power. There was never an era where you thought, Where’d Nicole Kidman go? And on top of being an incredible actress and movie star, she’s now a fashion icon and clubbing in Ibiza, and things like that. She seems like this ethereal presence on earth, which I think gives way for her to be the representation of cinema as ghosts in this show.

Mindelle: For me, it’s “That indescribable feeling” [from Kidman’s AMC pre-show ad]. There’s something about her “indescribable” that helped me tap into Nicole.

Zak: Nicole’s laugh. There’s nothing more infectious on screen or in an interview. There’s a super cut of her sneaking up on people on red carpets, where you’ll just see her hand enter the screen and, like, pull Laura Dern closely into her. Nicole’s red carpet star energy is just undeniable and a key thing in the world.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.
