#6637. Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

For 50 years, natural beauty company Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’. It was plastered on the office walls and repeated ad nauseam by staff, but had no legal footing. Then, in 2021, creative directors Simeon Rose and Anne Hopkins put the provocation to a group of groundbreaking legal experts: how could they turn the slogan into something more?

Enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head. Some companies appoint a nature director — a human proxy for nature, who holds a formal board seat, written into the company’s articles of association, with the same financial and legal duties as other board members. Others appoint nature guardians, who perform a similar role in advocating for nature at the board level, but they don’t necessarily have voting rights.

A new programme by Kering and the Centre for Sustainable Fashion hopes to reimagine how companies make high-level decisions, but is the industry ready to embrace change?

NOTB was proposed by Faith In Nature, and fleshed out by legal non-profits Lawyers for Nature and the Earth Law Center (ELC), but it was inspired by Indigenous communities who have practiced nature-centric governance for millennia. “The current business system is operating exactly as it was designed to: businesses pool capital, build goods and services at scale, speed and low cost, and accrue benefits for shareholders,” explains Mary Johnstone-Louis, senior fellow in management at the University of Oxford’s Saïd Business School. “Putting nature on the board is radical because it introduces a stakeholder on which every business depends, but whose interests are not typically represented at the board level.”

While there was no precedent for putting nature on the board, there were other case studies to draw on, says Lawyers for Nature co-founder and managing director Brontie Ansell. “Until relatively recently, women were seen as objects of law, rather than subjects of law. Like nature, they were not allowed to hold property, vote or voice concerns. Now, we look back on that with horror,” she explains. “Likewise, we are very familiar with widening the stakeholder pool in boardrooms. Many now include HR managers, union representatives, and health and safety officers. Extending this to nature is critical to human survival.”

Alongside Faith In Nature, NOTB has since been adopted by dozens of companies, including British interiors brand House of Hackney, Norwegian apparel brand Northern Playground, and French IT services company Norsys. Each has put their own spin on the blueprint, contributing to a fast-evolving consensus on best practices, and throwing open the doors for further innovation. Vogue Business invited these early adopters to share the tensions, toggles and opportunities.

Businesses are just as diverse and idiosyncratic as nature, says Faith In Nature managing director Hannah Whittaker. When it comes to putting nature on the board, each business has to do it in its own way.

NOTB encourages companies to give nature voting rights, but it’s possible to test nature governance without this. Outdoor apparel brand Patagonia made waves in 2022 when it created a nature purpose trust model, making a collection of environmental non-profits the beneficiary of 98% of its non-voting stock, while retaining approval rights in the Patagonia Purpose Trust, controlled by the family of founder Yvon Chouinard.

Approaches may also differ by jurisdiction, notes ELC’s nature governance business development associate Anna Solgaard, who acts as the nature guardian for Norwegian clothing label Northern Playground. Finding ways to give nature more legal rights requires “creative lawyering”, adds Alexandra Pimor, director of the ELC’s Nature Governance Agency. “That’s the beauty of nature on the board: we did not have to change the law to do it, we just changed our relationship with the law to give it a different purpose [taking existing rights for board members and extending them to nature]. In a capitalist environment, the corporate world is probably the easiest place to embed the voice of nature, because companies are given so much freedom.”

At Norsys, nature is both a director and a shareholder with a 10% stake in the business. “This is a strong model because it means nature will always be represented on the board, it’s not just one nomination we forget about in three years,” says the company’s nature director Frantz Gault, author of Nature at Work and co-founder of Vivøices, a public interest organization promoting the representation of the living world in organizational governance. Gault helped design the nature governance at Norsys, complementing his own role with a council of advisors, who also decide how dividends from nature’s 10% stake are spent.

Lawyers for Nature, on the other hand, prefers for nature directors to remain as “conflict-free” as possible. In the frameworks it has designed, nature representatives are not heavily salaried by the company, they don’t have a bonus linked to profit, they don’t owe the company money or vice versa, and they don’t have — or at least, they commit to disclosing — any other conflicts of interest. “By minimizing those conflicts, the nature representative can speak in the purest form possible about what nature needs,” says Ansell.

At Northern Playground, the articles of association include a “safety valve” whereby the nature proxy can be relieved of their duties if the company is approaching bankruptcy, to reduce the risk of them being held personally liable.

Another contention point is whether the nature proxy should have the right to veto strategic decisions, as well as voting on them. “If you get to the point where you need a veto, you’ve already lost,” says Dr Juliet Rose, head of development at the British botanical garden and research hub The Eden Project, and nature director at Faith In Nature. “You’re trying to get everybody moving in the same direction, so nobody even suggests something that would require a veto.”

At Norsys, Gault has the power to veto, but has never activated it. To keep the “nuclear power” in check, he is required to confer with a council of 10 scientific experts before taking a position in board meetings. Still, knowing the veto exists can be persuasive enough. “Everyone knows I have the power to veto, so the other directors listen when I speak, and they work with me to find a consensus.” If a veto isn’t on the cards, companies can implement the right to disagree, and the right to express that disagreement in public, adds Gault, or the right to resign. “These are little legal technicalities, but they help make nature’s voice more meaningful.”

Whichever approach a company chooses, Vivøices recommends running a year-long pilot before codifying nature’s role or communicating the program to consumers. “You do a pilot, then map the impact and what happened, how it changed the way decisions were made, how it influenced the culture internally, and what it means to really integrate the position of nature,” says co-founder Niels de Fraguier.

When House of Hackney advertised a directorship “for mother nature and future generations” in 2023, it received over 500 applications — its most popular job listing to date. But finding the right person to represent something as nebulous as nature was no small feat. “We had applications from scientists, teachers, poets and everything in between,” says House of Hackney co-founder Frieda Gormley, author of In the Company of Nature.

The challenge is finding someone who can bridge economic and ecological realities, says the University of Oxford’s Johnstone-Louis. “They have to protect the company, and at the same time, they have to speak for nature. That means they have to toggle between immediacy and long-termism; between business as usual and what business could be,” she says. Regardless of their professional background, humility and diplomacy are the key competencies, adds de Fraguier.

Both Faith In Nature and House of Hackney appointed Lawyers for Nature’s Ansell as their inaugural nature director, establishing the legal basis for the role and ironing out any kinks. Her successors have wildly different skill sets: Rose has a background in plant science and ecology, while House of Hackney’s nature director Charmian Love specializes in governance, having co-founded B Lab UK, the organization behind the B Corp certification. Love says her goal is to create tools that make it easier for more diverse nature proxies to step into the role in future, while Rose says her success is defined by how well she empowers staff throughout the company, so whoever holds the nature directorship is not working alone, or resting solely on their own, inevitably limited, experience.

Ideally, nature-centric decision-making cascades down through the company, and the nature director works in tandem with a well-established nature lead. While the former stewards the long-term purpose of the business, the latter embeds it in day-to-day operations. Without a nature director in their corner, a nature lead can easily fall into the same trap as sustainability leads, tasked with overhauling the business but lacking the resource or buy-in to do so, instead operating in a silo and trying to shoehorn change into business as usual. And without a nature lead to operationalize nature-centric decision-making, a nature director risks becoming little more than “window dressing”, says Johnstone-Louis.

To avoid tokenizing nature, Faith In Nature has designed a nature dashboard, which translates its goals into tangible projects each team can track progress against. Projects fall into five governing principles: governance, operational impact, sourcing, community and regeneration. “We had to work through the confusion and connect each team with the outcomes we wanted for nature, each of which has budgets, resources and KPIs attached,” explains Whittaker. “Otherwise, the concept can be quite theoretical for staff.” These projects span from changing the adhesive on labels to make at-home recycling easier, to running the brand’s first major television ad in collaboration with Channel 4 and B Corp.

At House of Hackney, Love starts every board meeting with a nature degradation pulse-check and a poem about nature, based on climate policy leader Nigel Topping’s remarks that “we need to be guided by science and moved by poetry”. Beyond board meetings, Love has defined 10 topics that are material to nature, from supply chain and procurement to regulatory changes and financial investments. Decisions about these topics are automatically escalated to a monthly nature meeting. She has also introduced a spin on the traditional ‘going concern test’ boards use to assess how nature-related decisions will affect the company’s future viability and license to operate.

On top of this, Love has a private email address where staff can discreetly voice concerns or ideas, and the company regularly invites inspirational nature-related speakers into the office. The next phase is to trial a physical card game, she says, which will live in every meeting room, encouraging staff to question their daily decision-making through a nature-centric lens, inspired by similar games at tea brand Pukka Herbs. And at the end of the year, House of Hackney will publish an open-source toolkit for NOTB, informed by its Greenprint fellowship, where 10 SMEs — including Lush, Davines and Vivobarefoot — experimented with nature governance over 12 months.

NOTB is not just another sustainability box for companies to tick; it’s a paradigm shift that goes beyond sustainability, toward regeneration.

“Philosophically, these are two very different landscapes,” explains Solgaard. “Sustainability is an anthropocentric paradigm, but nature is ecocentric, which means that the more-than-human world is valued alongside humans. Sustainability works with separation and reductionism, which is why we have all these boxes to tick, and we struggle to view things holistically, or to see how everything is interconnected. Nature is everything.”

Putting nature on the board also means moving beyond the risk mitigation approach that has defined so many corporate nature strategies, and underscored the business case for nature, to date, adds Johnstone-Louis. The risk mitigation approach asks how companies can continue to extract resources like cotton and wool pulp from nature, and reduce supply chain disruption from nature-related disasters like water scarcity and flooding. The NOTB approach — especially for companies like House of Hackney, which have combined nature with future generations — asks how decisions made today will affect the ability of future systems to thrive, sometimes looking as far ahead as seven generations. “It’s a different way of seeing the world,” she adds.

Addressing nature directly is a leap into the unknown — not least because so few companies have mapped their nature risks and dependencies. But rather than face this with fear, Pimor encourages companies to see the opportunities. “We are facing the most incredible, unprecedented ecological challenge. Facing the unknown means becoming more open to creativity, innovation and imagination. That’s what the voice of nature brings to the table.”

Deep transformation tends to be slow and steady, concludes Ansell. “Slow isn’t ideal in the situation we find ourselves in, but it’s better than going backwards. The idea here is for nature to be a gentle guiding voice, moving the rudder one degree at a time until the ship has completely changed course. It’s exciting. There’s so much still up for grabs in terms of distilling the theory and making it work for each individual sector or situation.”

#6636. Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” said Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in New York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

#6635. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6634. The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Launched in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

Much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Launched in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

When I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

Imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Launched in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere new—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

This was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Launched in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Launched in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Launched in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Launched in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

#6633. Ciara Has One Holiday Cooking Rule & You Really Don't Want To Break It

She's all for getting creative with Oreos, although she has much stronger feelings about the rest of the menu.

Ciara has one request for whoever’s in charge of Christmas dinner: Please, whatever you do, make sure you’re up for the assignment. She’s willing to embrace a little holiday mess, but apparently, there’s a limit to how far that generosity extends into the kitchen.

“All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”

Ciara, a mom of four, certainly understands how quickly the festivities can get away from you. “Christmas in our house is full of love, excitement and a little chaos,” she said in a statement. But when it comes to the actual Christmas menu, she’s got some traditions she’s pretty attached to, many of which go all the way back to her childhood in Atlanta, Georgia.

"If you know one thing about us ATLians, you have Thanksgiving on Christmas. The same meal comes back around again," she told Delish.

And we’re talking a serious Southern spread: turkey legs, mac and cheese, candied yams, collard greens, chitlins, and pig feet. She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara says those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

#6631. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6629. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6628. Ina Garten’s Dancing With The Stars Confession Has Me Mourning What Could’ve Been

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

“Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

#6627. “Focus on Learning”: Career Lessons With Burberry’s Daniel Lee and Anna Wintour

The morning after Vogue World 2026: Milano, all anyone online wanted to talk about was “the robots”. The moment became a lightning rod for memes, TikTok reactions, and questions about the state of creativity today. It turns out that was sort of the point.

A couple of months after the event, Anna Wintour, chief content officer at Condé Nast and global editorial director of Vogue, invited Burberry’s chief creative officer Daniel Lee to New York for a fireside chat at the Vogue Business Global Summit. Lee also wanted to talk about “the robots”.

A robot walks the runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026.

Of course, the two discussed much more than that, taking turns interviewing each other about Lee’s journey at the British brand during a company-wide turnaround, Wintour’s first job in fashion, the US midterms that happened the day before, and success — spoiler: social media makes it look easy. Ahead of the official announcement, Wintour also teased the Met Costume Institute’s theme for 2027: extraORDINARY.

Anna Wintour: Daniel, good morning. Thank you for coming all the way from London. So Daniel, you chose a very quiet news day here in the US. Have you been following the election news?

Daniel Lee: Yeah, definitely. I was super jet-lagged, so I was watching the news all night.

AW: I have to ask you, how do you think [Senator-elect] James Talarico would look in a Burberry suit?

DL: Well, I’d be happy to see anyone looking great in a Burberry suit.

Anna and Daniel on stage at the Vogue Business Global Summit.

AW: Very diplomatic. I guess you’re a Burberry ambassador. I read that you first thought you wanted to be a designer when your aunt took you to see the windows at Harvey Nichols in Leeds as a boy. I guess the equivalent over here would be Saks. Do you agree?

DL: Yes, I’m afraid that is true. You know, I didn’t fall into fashion by looking through pages of Vogue. That’s probably the story I should start saying. I mean, I grew up in the north of England in an area called Yorkshire, which is very beautiful — it’s in the countryside and very green. It rains a lot.

DL: David Hockney is from my hometown. Also, Christopher Bailey is from the same area [Yorkshire]. The Burberry trench coats are made in that area, so I guess Burberry was somehow ingrained in me since I was born. Clothes were really practical in my childhood. Fashion wasn’t something that was really part of my family or my upbringing. We wore clothes to stay warm and dry.

DL: Very Burberry. As kids, we liked to play outside. We would spend our childhood riding bikes in the rain, in Wellington boots. When Harvey Nichols opened in Leeds, I remember going past that store and seeing these incredible windows, and I guess I realized clothes could be so much more. It was like seeing a fantasyland. I guess that’s when I started to think this maybe could be a career for me.

DL: Eventually, yes. As a child, I think my first instinct was to get out of Yorkshire. As much as I love the countryside, I knew there was more. I was curious.

AW: Well, you did just buy a house there, so you must like it?

DL: You stay connected to your roots. But I think, as a 12-year-old, I went to London for the first time, and I remember seeing the variety of people in the streets, seeing the theater, so many things going on. I really wanted to be part of that culture. I think that’s what initially drew me to London and eventually to art school. I went to [Central] Saint Martins. I did an art foundation year, into fashion qualifications later on.

AW: OK. You’re meant to ask me a question now.

DL: Anna, what was your first job in fashion? And what did you learn from it?

AW: I’m going to talk about the first job that I actually enjoyed in fashion, which was working at Harper’s & Queen (now Harper’s Bazaar UK) in London, where there were two to three people — on a good day — in the fashion department. So I went in there, and I was immediately an editor, even though I had zero experience. I was always so very grateful for that training because there were no budgets. I do remember my boss once giving me maybe £10 or £20 and saying, ‘Anna, go to Morocco or go south. Find a sheikh, find a maharaja, and do a shoot.’ And somehow you did. It was just a different attitude. You had to be so creative and make things out of nothing. Because there were no teams at Harper’s & Queen, I learned how to do everything: you covered the market, you did the shoots, you wrote the captions.

When I came to New York, I went to work at Harper’s Bazaar [US]. I got fired fairly immediately because they told me I would never understand the American market, which is probably true. I then landed on my feet at New York Magazine, which was unbelievable training because I was working in a newsroom with guys like Nick Pileggi and Tom Wolfe — all the great writers of that time. They didn’t give a damn about what I did. They put me next to the bathrooms, so I got to see everybody coming in and out. Because nobody cared about fashion or style, they just left me alone. Eventually, I got a call from Condé Nast. It’s interesting when you talk to young people today how they’re focused on success, and they’re not focused on learning. Without the base, you can't succeed.

I’m meant to ask you a question now. So, congratulations on your very successful show in September. I think it was the first time you collaborated with anyone creatively, and the person that you chose to collaborate with is Celia Birtwell — she’s an 85-year-old legend in textile design, a partner to the great Ossie Clark. Did you have to do much convincing to get her involved? Maybe explain to our audience a little bit more about who she is.

DL: I would say Celia is probably mostly known as Ossie Clark’s collaborator in all those years of incredible dresses and work that I think is on every designer’s moodboard. And she was also very, very close friends with David Hockney and is a subject in many beautiful pieces of his work. We were celebrating 170 years of Burberry this year. We wanted to do the brand justice, and we were thinking of ways to do new things. I met with Celia, actually, just for a conversation. You never really know if someone’s going to be interested in working together. People are terrified by our timelines.

Textile designer Celia Birtwell with her partner and collaborator Ossie Clark in July 1971. Birtwell’s prints for Clark’s dresses are, in Daniel Lee’s words, “on every designer's moodboard.”

She came to the meeting saying, ‘You know, I’m really inspired by the check. I love the way Hockney paints ginghams on a tablecloth, the perspective that he gives to that.’ I said, ‘Well, would you be up for making some new work?’ And she did. She started with the checks, then the ginghams, and then the beautiful kind of English florals. Hockney gives me so much joy, emotion and warmth.

Birtwell’s new take on the brand’s check was inspired by the way David Hockney paints gingham on a tablecloth.

AW: Yeah, and he was so prolific, painting right up until the end, using an iPad, using different ways to make art. I’m sure you saw that last incredible show that was on at the Louis Vuitton Foundation in Paris. What a life. [Now] you’re meant to ask me…

DL: Congratulations on Vogue World: Milan. Would you like to talk about the robots?

AW: I’d love to. So the subject of Vogue World: Milan was our belief in the art of the human hand, the creativity of the hand, and the human mind in the age of technology. And we felt that to add something that represented technology, in a way that was — in my view — faintly ridiculous, reinforced the idea behind the theme of the exhibition. As is often in my case, not everyone agreed with me, but it certainly caused a lot of conversation.

Gigi Hadid at Vogue World: Milano. The show celebrated, in Anna Wintour’s words, “the art of the human hand” in the age of technology.

We’re moving on now to San Francisco in September, and we’re really going to be addressing the diversity and the incredible communities that live in San Francisco, and how it’s a city that has stood up for so much. The symphony and the museums there are extraordinary.

Talking about San Francisco, let’s talk about tech. Your last collection seemed to us that you were really advocating the celebration of imperfection and the romance of things made by hand. Is that true? And what do you feel about AI in terms of your creative work?

DL: As a child, I would spend my time making birthday cards, making cakes with my mom and making dance costumes for my sister. I’m a maker. Obviously I have a mobile phone, but tech is not a huge part of my life per se. I’m not a big computer gamer; I never even check email. I only really use WhatsApp.

DL: I think that’s what I love about luxury fashion. I really think luxury is about preservation of this savoir-faire, this craftsmanship. One of the main roles of the creative directors and companies today is to preserve that know-how and make it relevant, so that customers today can appreciate it.

OK, Anna, could you tell us more about next year’s Costume Institute show?

AW: Absolutely. It’s going to be extraordinary.

Daniel, I think it’s five years that you’ve been at Burberry?

AW: You went into a company that was in disarray, and looking at it from the outside, maybe not very well run. Two years ago, CEO Joshua Schulman came in. That must have been very welcome to have a good partner. He’s been integral — led by your creativity — to Burberry’s unbelievable turnaround. What is it like to work with Josh?

DL: Josh brought an incredible energy, passion, and belief in Burberry. He loves the brand, and his energy really reverberates in the company. I think that’s the role of a great leader. Josh brought a lot of discipline to the brand. He really grew up in American department stores; he intimately understands wholesalers and has very personal relationships with them.

Daniel Lee, Anna Wintour and Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman. Lee credits Schulman, who joined two years ago, with bringing “discipline” and a clear pricing strategy to the brand’s turnaround.

AW: I remember being in your store on a Saturday morning looking for something for a small child, and he was there, folding the scarves.

DL: We laugh, but Josh spends his vacations in malls. We had an executive dinner and were asked about our favorite places, and I’m sure he mentioned a mall in California. When he arrived, he brought a very clear idea around price architecture.

Anna, what do you think the British fashion industry needs at the moment?

AW: I think they need to really focus on who they are. We all look to London for creativity and individuality — and a degree of eccentricity. There’s a freedom to the way you see the kids dressed in the streets there that is the antithesis of American or cool Italian, more luxury dressing. It’s a little bit closer to what I was saying when I first was working in London, when you had to do everything.

I think that the British Fashion Council really needs to focus on that and make more noise about what you can see in London that you cannot see anywhere else. They have a great brand like Burberry, and it was so wonderful to see McQueen back in London and Christopher Kane at Mulberry.

They have so many creative kids, students, who can’t get jobs there, so they need to make sure that London becomes more of a global fashion mecca — that the retailers, the CEOs, and the journalists go. [Prime Minister] Andy Burnham seems like he’s going to be much more open to business in the UK, and they need to lean on what they own.

Burberry Spring/Summer 2027, a collection that celebrates handcraft and the brand’s 170th year.

So, the last shows were followed by quite a few creative director departures and appointments. How do you see this constant creative shuffle shaping the industry?

DL: My experience is that it takes time to understand and have a dialogue with the company that you work for, understand the archive, the culture, the people. It also takes time to build a team, and people need stability. I advocate for continuity. Also, when there are constant aesthetic shifts, it’s hard for the customer to understand that. I think there are moments where things do need to be revolutionized, and change is needed. Change is good. But too much change is discombobulating. It’s incredibly hard when you join a brand.

What do you think is the future of what we used to call magazines?

AW: I was doing an interview with Grace Coddington, who’s worked at Vogue for so many years, and we were reminiscing about when we were only working on print. She was able to go off to these extraordinary locations for what seems like an unthinkable amount of time — probably only with £20 in her pocket. She would go to Scotland for 10 days; she would go to China for two weeks. There was a great luxury in being able to have time to plan and think about what an issue of Vogue should look like. But it was a very narrow audience. When I first arrived at Vogue, people would disappear in the afternoons because they were going to Jones Beach — there just wasn’t that much to do.

Anna Wintour and Grace Coddington. Recalling their print days, Wintour remembers when Coddington could spend 10 days shooting in Scotland or two weeks in China. That was “a great luxury,” she says, but for a much narrower audience.

How lucky are we now to have all these amazing platforms to talk to our audiences? Our audiences have grown to unthinkable numbers. One of the great experiences and joys of what I do now is helping Adam [Baidawi, GQ’s global editorial director], Chloe [Malle, American Vogue’s head of editorial content], and Chioma [Nnadi, British Vogue’s head of editorial content], and all the editors that I work with over the world.

This afternoon, I’m leaving for Asia to work with our editors in Japan, China, Taiwan, and beyond. And I learn a lot from all of them. You have to be on the ground. I really feel that it’s so important to understand different cultures and how they think and work. I remember years and years ago, when I was first starting out, a great friend of mine said, ‘Anna, wherever you are, you have to walk in the street, climb a high point, visit a museum, and have a cup of coffee.’ I always remember that. I think sometimes when people get successful, they don’t walk in the street. When you walk in the street, that’s when you see the world.

What advice do you give those who want to become creative directors? Do you think social media has distorted the way young creatives see their trajectory by making them think they can be their own boss, or do you think it’s a good thing?

DL: I think social media makes things look very easy. People don’t always see the journey: the highs, the lows, the learnings. I don’t think you should set out to be an overnight success or to have instant gratification on social media. I’ve been every level, every part of a studio. I’ve been the intern, the pattern maker, the design director. I’ve lived all those jobs, and I’ve had those experiences, and that helps me do the job I do today.

AW: This is an audience of mostly executives. What’s one piece of advice you would give to them when it comes to working with creative teams?

DL: I think empathy is very important, respect is very important, understanding is important, and humility. No one’s right all the time. My favorite kind of working relationship is when it feels collaborative. I think as a creative leader, I try to create a space and framework to allow people to feel safe. I think this is something I once heard you say: ‘You hire great people, and you let them work.’ Trust is important.

#6626. 8 Best Nose Hair Trimmers GQ's Editors Have Tested in 2026

Perhaps it never occurred to you that you might need a list of the best nose hair trimmers until this very moment. Fear not—reasonably priced, speedily shipped (thanks, Amazon), simple-to-use options populate this list of our favorites. Meaning—whenever you have a general facial hair emergency that calls for rogue hair removal, you need not add an ear hair trimmer or brow trimmer to your cart. You need only think back to this moment and thank your lucky stars for choosing a gadget to cut hair—wherever it may appear.

Similar to other battery-operated beard trimmers, back shavers, razors, hair clippers, or body hair trimmers, these trimmers are ergonomic and designed with durability in mind. You can use many of them on wet or dry hair to trim nose hair, and like other electric razors you may be familiar with, most can actually be used for nose & ears (and also as eyebrow trimmers).

If you’re looking for a quick, pain-free way to get rid of unwanted nose whiskers, Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer Series 5000 can absolutely handle that. But this versatile grooming device also covers most hair-detailing needs with precision and gusto. Add in the affordable price, and that’s why it stands as our pick for the best nose hair trimmer, bar none.

The 5000 Series includes three types of trimmers: a linear-style trimmer, plus the rotary and detail attachments. Depending on your preference, you can use either the linear or rotary trimmer for both nose and ear hairs as well as working as an eyebrow trimmer. Personally, I appreciate the size of the cylinder on the rotary trimmer, which is wider than most and is able to capture overgrown hairs better than any other trimmer I tested. The linear trimmer works great at managing eyebrows (thanks to two different guard lengths) and tending to fuzzy ear canals. Perhaps the unsung hero of the kit is the straight-edge detail trimmer, which is more than capable of daily touch-ups. Think sideburns, mustaches, or even edging beards in a pinch.

The 5000 Series is battery-powered, cordless, easy to wash with a rinse in the bathroom sink, and you already know that anything made from Philips Norelco has longevity. If what you’re after is a no-frills device to manage most facial hair needs, consider this trimmer twenty bucks well spent. Adam Hurly

True to its name, Wahl’s Micro Groomsman is easily the smallest nose hair trimmer we recommend—but don’t let its diminutive size fool you. This is a perfectly pared-down trimmer that’s great for home use, and even better for travel. Heck, it’s so small you might forget you stashed it in your dopp kit.

The Micro Groomsman offers two interchangeable heads, including a rotary trimmer for nose and ears, and a linear trimmer for detailed work. You can also attach an eyebrow guard to manage any overgrown caterpillars up top. The compact design feels great in the hand, and the stainless steel blades are cinch to clean. Even if you have a primary grooming device you love, we readily recommend the Wahl Micro Groomsman as a go-to backup option or a permanent accessory in your travel kit. Adam Hurly

Got a partner who absolutely hates when you leave trimmed hair in the sink? This one’s for you. An upgrade from the standard Panasonic ER-GN30 (shown in the video), this trimmer offers everything you’d want from a dedicated nose hair trimmer, but what sets it apart is a vacuum system that sucks up clippings in an instant. Easy clean-up, yes, but the vacuum system also helps prevent bacteria build-up. We call that a win-win.

Otherwise, this tool is fairly minimal with no fancy attachments. You get a rotary trimmer, and that’s all. Granted, it’s a powerful one that’s able to mow down the coarsest strands. All told, the GN70-K is best for the person who just needs a dependable nose and ear trimmer that will save them from the mess. Adam Hurly

A whole grooming kit is excessive if all you need to tackle is the occasional nose hair. But if you’re also maintaining a beard, tidying body hair, or cutting your own hair, Philips’ 9000 starts to make much more sense. The current kit has 23 tools and accessories, including a nose and ear head, with a stainless-steel handle and rubber grip. Philips rates it for up to six hours between charges.

Long-term testing notes: Philips' previous iteration of the Multigroom 9000 was my go-to grooming tool. Alas, I only realized how much I relied on its nose hair shaving attachment after I lost the thing. Now there's a new (albeit broadly similar) update of the same device, and I'm back to trimming as much hair as humanly possible with one device. My advice for anyone else who picks up this trimmer? Be sure to check every piece when packing up after a trip. Adam Hurly

My nose hairs have become alarmingly ambitious with age, which is unfortunate given how little enthusiasm I have for plucking, waxing, or the local Turkish barber’s fire tricks. The Weed Whacker 3.0 Pro, thankfully, gets the job done with considerably less drama. Alongside its rotary nose and ear head, there’s a separate eyebrow blade with a 2mm comb. USB-C charging saves another proprietary cable, and the travel lock stops it switching on in your bag.

Long-term testing notes: During my review testing, the rotary head cut through my thick, wiry hairs quickly, without the pulling and sneezing fits I’ve experienced with cheaper trimmers. It was still ticklish, but the compact head was easy to maneuver around my nostrils and ears. The LED helped in my dimly lit bathroom, showing hairs I might otherwise have missed. I also liked the solid-feeling matte-black handle and how easily it rinsed clean. The claimed hour of runtime held up in testing, too. It’s the best dedicated nose trimmer I’ve used. Esat Dedezade

If you have a beard and your grooming routine requires a more exacting tool, ConairMan’s Nose and Ear Trimmer kit will serve you well. I think of this more as a mustache and beard-line tidier-upper, as opposed to a nose hair trimmer.

The tool has a rotary blade that makes quick work of nostril hairs. But its two-faced trimming and shaving head is its best calling card—you get a straight-edge detailer on one side, and a shaver on the other. If you’re looking for a tool that can truly tend to the lower half of your face, ConairMan offers an excellent package that’ll get the job done. Adam Hurly

Philips’ 7000 costs less than the 9000 above and still covers far more than nose hair. The US kit includes 22 tools and accessories, with a precision comb for short facial hair and heads for wider grooming jobs. Finding somewhere to keep all those small parts is part of the deal.

My main complaint, as always, is the proprietary charging connection. The supplied cable plugs into USB-A at the other end, but you still need Philips’ cable to charge the trimmer. Braun, Remington, and other brands are just as guilty of this, by the way.

Long-term testing notes: In my three-week test of the 7000, its nose and ear attachment cut comfortably without pulling, snagging, or irritation. It was much less unpleasant than plucking. The wider kit also earned its place on my chest and underarms, so the extra attachments felt useful. Esat Dedezade

If you already have a Panasonic MultiShape, the nose-trimming head gives its rechargeable handle another job. It swaps with the system’s beard trimmer, shaver, and toothbrush heads, so there’s one less complete gadget to pack when you travel.

For a new buyer, the lithium-ion handle and nose head cost around $81.99 together. The $21.99 attachment won’t work on its own, and the other heads cost extra. That makes the MultiShape easier to justify if you’ll use more of the system. For nose hair alone, a dedicated trimmer is a simpler buy.

Long-term testing notes: During several weeks with a broader MultiShape kit, I found the nose head cleared unwanted hair without pain or friction. The lightweight handle was comfortable, and switching from trimming to shaving or brushing his teeth took little effort. That ease of moving between jobs made the system particularly useful for travel. The handle and nose head linked here are sold separately from the other attachments he used. Owen Gough

While many nose hair trimmers tout motors with serious RPMs and boast about their long battery life, the truth is, you won’t be using it much—maybe once every couple weeks for a mere 5 or 10 seconds. But that’s no excuse to skimp on them, either. Here are a few things to consider:

We’ve tested all manner of nose hair trimmers for this guide, from simple battery-powered models to grooming kits with interchangeable heads. We look at how comfortably they cut, whether they pull or miss hairs, and how easy they are to handle and clean. Extra attachments need to be useful, and we consider battery life and charging alongside performance.

The guide draws on Adam Hurly’s years of grooming reviews and Ian Burke’s experience of living with the Zorami trimmer long after receiving it as a joke gift. My additions bring in testing for British GQ, alongside Owen Gough’s assessment of the MultiShape system. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation. You can read more about our editorial standards at About GQ.

The best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is important to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

If visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

To trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:

The cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” says Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more important that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”

Simone (who is professionally mononymous) is a celebrity men’s groomer. Her A-List clients include Mahershala Ali, Ramy Youssef, Jason Schwartzman, John Magaro, and Brandon Perea.

Adam Hurly has been covering men's grooming for GQ since 2016. He also writes about travel. Adam is a Sioux Falls, SD native, University of Kansas graduate, former New Yorker, and current expat in Berlin. His favorite season is Oscar Season, his favorite book is Dinner At the Homesick Restaurant, and he is a proud superfan of Survivor.
