This photograph is part of the series ‘Rotting from Within’. Beginning at seventeen, when he reconnected with his estranged father, Abdulhamid Kircher turned to photography to make sense of his family history and his own Turkish heritage. Combining portraits, candid observations, archival material and personal writings, he traces the generational trauma passed down through the men in his family, confronting the myths of masculinity, violence and inherited identity. Part autobiography, part visual investigation, the work explores how photography can help us approach the people closest to us, even when their histories remain partly unknowable.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Mannequins’. Using taxidermy as an unexpected departure point, the artist examines sculptural form within narrative imagery to reflect on aging, inherited femininity, and the labor behind entertainment. Moving between taxidermied figures and intimate portraits of herself and her mother, the work draws a piercing parallel between preserved animal specimens and the expectations placed on young women in Hollywood: rendered pristine, suspended in time, and meticulously packaged for consumption. Part conceptual study, part personal inquiry, the series interrogates the artifice of beauty and the cost of eternal preservation.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Moon in Your Throat’. Asking what happens to the grief swallowed in pursuit of success, the work depicts Koreans living across the United States seated inside darkened homes, illuminated only by the faint glow of refrigerators, screens, and digital clocks. Through long-exposure portraits, contemplative still lifes, and family-photo collages, the artist explores how displacement, collective history, and unresolved emotion physically inhabit the body. Guided by the Korean concept of Han and Jung’s archetype of the shadow, the series creates a quiet space for collective mourning, asking what transformative healing might emerge when buried sorrows are finally permitted to surface.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Room 房间’. Drawn from the artist’s life lived between Chengdu and New York, the work gathers tender glimpses of friends, lovers, and intimate, familiar interiors. Originally published as their debut photobook in 2025, the series functions as an architecture constructed entirely through imagery and deliberate pairings, tracing how the concept of home gradually evolved from a fixed physical location into a portable emotional state. Part visual diary, part spatial meditation, the photographs reflect on transience, connection, and the quiet spaces we assemble within ourselves to belong.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Effigy of Man’. A decade after his passing, the artist’s grandfather endures in family photographs as a revered, often feared patriarch—a strict, orthodox figure whose temperament was indelibly forged by his displacement from Multan to Haryana during the 1947 Partition of British India. Through studio portraiture and physical collage, the artist directly intervenes in these inherited portraits to challenge dominant codes of masculinity embedded in family archives. Part reckoning, part tender excavation, the work unpicks the myth of the unyielding patriarch, suggesting that one must dismantle the monument of a man in order to truly see him.

This photograph is part of the series ‘MY HEAD IS A DESERT FULL OF TULIPS’. Conceived as an ongoing photographic universe suspended between reality and fiction, the work captures subjects suspended in media res, leaving their relationships, histories, and interior motives deliberately unresolved. Through recurring gestures, shared hairstyles, synchronized clothing, and uncanny everyday scenarios, disparate people and landscapes begin to rhyme and echo across frames, building a fractured, collective realm. Part cinematic daydream, part surrealist taxonomy, the series distills the tension between isolation and kinship, showing how easily the familiar can tilt into the strange, the intimate, and the absurd.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Ohnmacht’. Exploring the visceral experience of losing control over one’s body—a state of profound helplessness—the work captures women collapsing inward, where the tactile softness of their clothing clashes against stark, unforgiving environments to lay bare the weight of feminine expectations. Drawing from archival imagery of Victorian fainting spells and histories of mass hysteria, the artist uses shifting warm and cold light to expose the contradictory faces of disempowerment: fragile beauty, desperate cries for help, and latent resistance. Part psychological study, part quiet protest against patriarchal structures, the series gives tangible, enduring form to a silent exhaustion known intimately by women across generations.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Puerpera’. Born from the artist’s own birth trauma and the amnesia that enveloped the hours immediately following labor, the work offers a visceral exploration of a profound, near-universal threshold in womanhood: the disorienting stillness that arrives right after giving birth. Through intimate imagery, recorded conversations, and contemplative reflection, the series attempts to reconstruct an emotional landscape so intense, fleeting, and overwhelming that memory itself often fractures. Part personal catharsis, part raw maternal record, the project gives voice to the unspoken shock and tender vulnerability of early postpartum, reclaiming a physical reality too often eclipsed by silence.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Neti È Kon’. Translating into "The Night is Coming," the work documents nocturnal portraits and nocturnal scenes across Suriname, capturing the enigmatic spirit of the evening through the cultural cadence of its local dialect. Imbued with a quiet intimacy where darkness evokes memory and longing, the photographs examine the subtle sensory elements that trigger a sense of belonging, redefining home not as a fixed geographical border, but as an emotional construct carried within. Part cultural ode, part lyrical meditation on displacement and longing, the series reveals how the twilight hours can bridge distance and resurrect familiar worlds.

This video is part of the series ‘Hands, trees, heads, scars’. Conceived as a tender meditation on care, active listening, and hope, the work examines the fragile geography of skin and scars among amputated Ukrainian soldiers undergoing rehabilitative massage therapy in Lviv. Continuing their long-term research into relational dynamics within healthcare, Alberto Gottardo and Francesca Sironi quietly observe the gestures of solace exchanged between international practitioners and recovering servicemen like Sergei and his peers. Part clinical witness, part intimate humanitarian tribute, the series captures the quiet dignity of recovery, demonstrating how touch can transform sites of violent trauma into spaces of profound resilience and connection. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the series ‘Reconfigurations’. Conceived as an unbound portfolio of black-and-white figure studies, the work deliberately unsettles classical conventions of nude photography. Employing a split-field diopter, the camera folds the human form back onto itself, dissolving the boundaries between nearness and distance, the sensuous and the grotesque. Across eighteen loose, unsequenced prints, the project invites the viewer to touch, reorder, and physically recompose the imagery, transforming passive spectatorship into tactile engagement and leaving both the anatomical body and the act of looking open to endless reconfiguration.

This photograph is part of the series ‘D,D&D’. Framing the examination of one’s own life as an intentional act of role-play, the project stages an alliterative rite of passage where subconscious dreams and primal drives are confronted to forge inner strength. Moving through the shadow worlds of darkrooms and the grit of dirt, the artist harnesses photography to declare vulnerability while demanding personal power—meeting internal demons, owning forbidden desires, confronting and reshaping paternal lineage, and learning to dance with fear rather than submit to it. The series chronicles years of dedicated discipline and ritual transformation, insisting that one can actively draw destiny rather than remain doomed to it.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I owe you’. Approaching physical and emotional pain not as an isolating affliction but as a shared human threshold, the project considers discomfort as an unexpected site for connection, cooperation, and mutual care. Combining still photography and moving image, the artist studies how individuals navigate enduring suffering through subtle physical gestures, repetitive daily routines, intimate healing rituals, and collective support practices. Rather than fixating on the sensational depiction of hurt, the work investigates the quiet architectures of trust and vulnerability that emerge when bodies rely on one another through dependence, tenderness, and shared endurance.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Joyless Sex’. Chronicling the quiet desolation of intimacy unmoored from desire, the work lays bare the unvarnished realities of clandestine side hustles, the claustrophobia of lingering in rooms with lovers already outgrown, and the fragile currency of relationships alternately discarded and desperately preserved. Photographed across Paris and New York from 2018 to the present day, the series captures the raw friction between loneliness and physical proximity in modern metropolises. Part unflinching diary, part contemporary social record, the images excavate the silent compromises, hidden transactions, and enduring vulnerabilities that shape life behind closed apartment doors.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Crossing the River by Feeling the Stones’. Rooted in a concealed bodily experience from childhood, the project charts an intimate investigation into personal desire, latent fantasy, and emerging sexuality. Moving through a tender, playful, and deliberately clumsy visual navigation, the artist traces the fluid transformations of desire as it encounters migration, displacement, and restless curiosity. The project completely reimagines the female form, liberating the body from the confines of conventional gazes and reclaiming it as a sovereign territory of exploration and self-possession.

That Moment When You Can See The Crack In The World

This photograph is part of the series ‘That Moment When You Can See the Crack in the World’. Using the human body as mutable raw material, the work navigates the terrain of metamorphosis, queerness, and the porous boundary separating conventional beauty from monstrosity. Within this altered universe, reality becomes elastic and physical forms are liberated from prescriptive aesthetics, recasting the deemed "abnormal" not as an aberration, but as a fertile site for radical reimagining. The series celebrates physical disruption as a portal, exposing the fissures in our rigid societal architecture to glimpse alternative ways of being.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Near’. Bringing people, bodies, and everyday objects into unexpected physical configurations, the work allows familiar forms to dismantle their everyday functions and take on radical new possibilities. By deliberately loosening the rigid grip of established social identities, inherited norms, and conventional values, the artist constructs an open, liminal space of encounter. The series invites the individual to step beyond prescribed ways of being, creating a rare clearing where one might encounter the self—and the other—entirely anew.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Self-Portraits of No One’. Begun in 2013 prior to the artist’s gender transition, this ongoing photographic archive utilizes their own body as both subject and canvas across domestic interiors, untamed landscapes, and staged performances to interrogate identity, visibility, and physical metamorphosis. Resisting the tidy impulse of a linear transition narrative, the work approaches self-portraiture as a radical assertion of agency—reclaiming complete visual authorship over how the evolving body is documented, perceived, and remembered. The series reflects on the fluidity of becoming, demonstrating that the self is an open, ever-shifting horizon rather than a fixed destination.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Dublin Girls’. Exploring contemporary Irish girlhood through portraits captured across the artist’s hometown, the project is intimately rooted in her lived experience as an older sister and young Irish woman navigating sisterhood, identity, and the tender, quieter thresholds of coming of age. Moving beyond reductive cultural stereotypes and performative notions of femininity, the work captures its subjects in unvarnished authenticity, preserving an essential archive of what it feels like to discover and inhabit oneself in modern Dublin. The series celebrates the quiet resilience, vulnerability, and kinship forged on familiar streets.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Muted Ember’. The project observes younger generations navigating life in contemporary China as economic uncertainty fractures the long-held promise of steady upward mobility. Through quiet portraits and observational scenes, the work captures the quiet anxieties, disillusionment, and resilience of youth confronting a rapidly shifting social reality. Part generational portrait, part contemporary document, the series examines the tension between inherited aspirations and an uncertain future.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Sacrilegio’. Using constructed photography, the project reinterprets standard biblical imagery through the lens of modern Mexico and its northern border. By blending sacred iconography with popular culture, the work explores how religious symbols mutate when confronted with realities of violence, gender, and territorial power. Rather than challenging faith, it captures the living, breathing contradictions of contemporary devotion.

Anna Göldi: Memoria di una Strega, Rituale di Restituzione

This photograph is part of the series ‘Anna Göldi: Memoria di una Strega, Rituale di Restituzione’. The project stems from the historical tragedy of Anna Göldi, navigating the distance between archival records and the enduring resonance of her myth. Moving between reality and imagination, the imagery opens a symbolic space of restitution where her presence and memory can be reclaimed and told anew.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Fade into you.’. Combining original photography with subtitle stills drawn from popular media, the work uses cropping, sequencing, and visual treatment to detach familiar imagery from its initial context. Reconstructed into an altered narrative, the series examines how meaning degrades, shifts, and transforms as it circulates through systems of cultural reproduction.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Set in Stone’. The work captures the tender, fleeting connections found in daily life, grounding delicate emotions into permanence by printing the imagery directly onto stone. By anchoring transient intimacy to an unyielding surface, the series suggests that even the softest feelings leave enduring traces, holding a weight and memory that outlast time itself.

This video is part of the series ‘tranSformarse’. Moving from the safe enclosure of early beginnings to the inevitable compulsion to shed one’s skin, the work serves as an ode to blooming out of step, in one's own authentic hues. By leaving behind inherited expectations to embrace the painful, miraculous nature of metamorphosis, the series stands as a vital reminder that to truly inhabit the world is, at its bravest, a lifelong act of self-transformation. Watch Full Video Here

EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me)

This photograph is part of the series ‘EL TIGRE ME PERSIGUE (The Tiger Pursues Me)’. Created by Alcira Angelo, the project is an intimate photographic odyssey that explores self-discovery through the emotional and psychological terrain of duelo—a concept evoking both inner struggle and the reckoning that follows loss. The work unfolds as a visual dialogue with the self and others, constructing a quiet yet insistent collective portrait of grief and resilience.

This photograph is part of the series ‘My friend, Whisky’. The project chronicles the eight-year creative bond between photographer Fee-Gloria Grönemeyer and her muse and collaborator, Whisky Boonjongrux. Having developed multiple photographic dialogues together that consistently push both toward new creative horizons, the series stands as an intimate reflection on artistic trust, mutual growth, and the quiet courage required to be wholly oneself.

This photograph is part of the series ‘UNCOOL’. A study in visibility, embodiment, and representation, the project brings together twenty-seven portraits of individuals with disabilities and visible physical differences. Informed by the artist’s lived experience as a wheelchair user, the work examines how bodies are perceived, categorized, and normalized through imagery, critically questioning which bodies are granted visibility, under what conditions, and through which prevailing visual conventions.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Matriphagie’. The project investigates how societal structures transmit and internalize prescribed norms of femininity from an early age. Structured around interviews and encounters with young girls aged four to eleven, the work uses their testimonies—balancing between learned clichés and instinctive transgressions—to ground a visual inquiry into the ambivalences, tensions, and shifting definitions of the feminine.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Look at me like you love me’. Informed by the artist’s identity as a queer, nonbinary individual, the work explores the complexities of personhood, desire, intimacy, and family. Motivated by an existential search for self-understanding and human connection, the project centers on the radical necessity of living authentically and the mutual power of seeing and being seen, using intimate storytelling to invite viewers into deep reflection on their own identities and relationships.

This photograph is part of the series ‘t-fags’. Bringing together photographs and interviews with trans men, transmasculine, and non-binary people who identify with the reclaimed term ‘fag’, the project explores masculinities that openly embrace femininity and gender expansiveness. By challenging heteronormative expectations around gender transition, the work documents a community asserting radical self-definition. Created between 2022 and 2025, the series was self-published as a limited-edition artist book in 2026, serving as a vital archive of contemporary queer identity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘People’. Built on friendship, attraction, and creative collaboration, this ongoing portrait project actively reclaims who is pictured as desirable and who holds the authority behind the lens. Centering disabled subjects through the perspective of a gay, disabled photographer, the work employs nudity, fashion, and playful experimentation to capture beauty infused with sexual confidence, humor, and unfiltered desire.

This photograph is part of the series ‘I Love My Friends But They Are Killing Me’. The project examines contemporary beauty standards and their psychological toll through portraits of young Indian women navigating micro-celebrity—influencers, reality television figures, and aspiring actors pictured inside their private bedrooms and homes. Shot primarily on 35mm film with harsh direct flash and framed by episodic, reality-TV-style text, the work strikes a deliberate tension between cultural critique, intimate vulnerability, and biting absurdity.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Cut from the Street’. The project examines hair as a medium of self-expression, identity, and resistance among young men across north and central Chennai. Through portraits and interviews, the work interrogates how caste, class, skin tone, and urban geography dictate who is granted social legitimacy and visibility. Highlighting how identical aesthetics celebrated as fashion on privileged bodies are condemned as “indecent” or suspicious on others, the series reveals everyday styling as an act of defiance—a vital claim to presence and the right to be seen.

This photograph is part of the series ‘TOPS’. Extending the world of the companion short film, the work gathers intimate moments captured before, during, and after production to trace the profound physical and emotional journey of top surgery. Through quiet, behind-the-scenes glimpses, the collection documents the urgency of gender-affirming care, the essential networks of community support that sustain it, and the deep vulnerability that shapes the path toward embodied self-realization.

The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back

This photograph is part of the series 'The Water Bring We, The Water Wanna Take We Back', a project that explores the Gullah Geechee corridor as a landscape of memory, survival, and spiritual continuity. Drawing on a Gullah proverb and the Bakongo cosmogram, the project examines water as both rupture and return—marking histories of the Middle Passage while sustaining cultural resilience. Through photographs of the Low Country, the work considers how Geechee communities navigate displacement, climate change, and enduring ancestral presence.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Who’s Afraid of the Bad Wolf?’. Documenting the bedroom as the foundational universe of childhood, the work explores a space where solitude, play, and resilience are first tested, and where fantasy and reality seamlessly coexist. Centered on the intimate bedtime rituals invented by children to cultivate safety and ward off fear, the ongoing archive currently traces the private domestic worlds of eleven children across Piedmont, Italy.

This photograph is part of the series ‘An Anatomy of Fear’. Reflecting on fear as a collective condition shaped by uncertainty, instability and the accelerating pace of contemporary life, Alvaro Deprit explores the fragile territory between identity and transformation. Through images of unfinished clay and plaster sculptures, alongside the students who inhabit the art school where the work was made, he draws a parallel between bodies and forms in the process of becoming. Adolescence emerges as a particularly charged moment of this transition, when identity remains fluid and the boundaries between vulnerability and possibility are still being negotiated.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Thoughts, Feelings, Behaviour’. Begun in 2024, the project employs staged photography to interrogate narcissistic self-image, emotional isolation, and the alienating demands of the capitalist attention economy. Exploring the fraught boundary between self-sufficiency and raw vulnerability, the work navigates currents of desire, aggression, and melancholy. Through an experimental synthesis of body paint, collage, and sculptural props, the imagery blurs the lines between lens-based practice, painting, and tactile material experience.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Ọ Hụrụ M’—translating to “She Saw Me” in the artist’s native tongue, Igbo. Conceived as an intimate dialogue across her past, present, and future selves, this self-portrait project treats the camera lens as both a transformative portal and an unbound playground. Navigating life as a young Nigerian woman raised in the United States, the artist claims absolute authorship over her representation. Standing firmly as both creator and subject, she transforms self-imaging into a sovereign act of agency, radical ownership, and resistance against cultural erasure.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Rose Sarajevo: Girls from the East’. Weaving together portraits of young women, local architecture, and surrounding nature, the project traces the enduring scars of conflict across an urban landscape under quiet reconstruction—most visibly marked by the “Sarajevo Roses,” mortar damage filled with red resin to memorialize fallen lives. Guided by fragmented memories, the artist undertakes an intimate quest for the origins of her own identity, using photography as an act of personal and historical reconciliation, an attempt to mend and bridge the fractures of time.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Home Story’. Combining documentary and staged photography, the project unearths fragmented, visceral narratives within a space fundamentally promised as a sanctuary: the domestic home. Acknowledging the difficulty of articulating trauma into daily reality, the work interrogates how patriarchal structures isolate survivors of domestic violence into silenced, individualized tragedies. By confronting the quiet complicity of institutional secrecy, the imagery functions as an act of disclosure—insisting that giving voice to these hidden experiences dismantles the systemic machinery that thrives on their suppression.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Scarlet Spirit’. Grounded in the enduring legacy of the 1947 Partition of India, the project traces the artist’s familial migration through ancestral memory and oral histories gathered across Kolkata’s refugee colonies. Synthesizing contemporary portraits, archival material, and surreal visual metaphors, the work constructs a layered archive of displacement that interrogates severed roots, cultural erasure, and collective resilience. Created in resonance with the milestone commemorations of Partition, the series links generational trauma and the arduous labor of rebuilding to the broader, ongoing realities of global displacement today.

The Drying Leaves: A Domestic Cartography Initiative

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Drying Leaves : A Domestic Cartography Initiative’. Set beneath the ancestral neem tree of Suktara, the work adopts the seasonal descent of winter leaves as a poignant metaphor for the passage of time and human mortality. Through a three-dimensional visual approach that weaves together photography, family archives, and spoken histories, the initiative maps intimate domestic geographies to resist alienation and stave off the "third death"—the quiet disappearance that occurs when a person’s name is spoken for the very last time.

This video is part of the series ‘Everything I Am or Have Since Become’. Centering on the elemental nature of water as a metaphor for queer safety—at once life-giving sanctuary and volatile peril—the project weaves together collective oral histories, writings, and movement developed collaboratively with an all-queer cast and crew. Created by diasporic artists navigating New York City in resistance to systemic precarity, the work follows three figures across aquatic terrains in ritualistic choreography. Through sustained cycles of grief, repetition, and bodily rebirth, the series meditates on the search for refuge in hostile environments, embodying the fluid, precarious nature of both sanctuary and identity. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the project ‘Driving License’. Exploring an online subculture where people buy and sell photographs of other people’s faces to use as their own, Lean Lui examines the shifting boundaries between identity, ownership and authenticity in the digital age. Through a three-month investigation in which she actively participated in these transactions, Lui explores how a face can become a commodity, a disguise or a new identity altogether. The work questions what it means to be seen, and whether an image can stand in for a person who does not exist.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Mixed / Unmistakably You’. Created by Norwegian-Indian artist Dev Dhunsi, the project takes the artist’s own mixed heritage as an inquiry into the nuances of cultural and personal identity. In a society where language lacks a direct term for mixedness, the work pairs photography and text to articulate experiences that have long remained unnamed. Interrogating how belonging, visibility, and intimacy are mediated by race, gender, and desire, the series constructs a luminous visual vocabulary for self-definition beyond existing cultural lexicons.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Constructed Portrait’. In an era marked by frictionless image oversaturation, the project investigates the blurred boundaries between the tangible and the synthetic. Confronting the extractive reality of digital photography—where personal images are systematically harvested as training data for artificial intelligence—the artist restricts the source material strictly to their own intimate photo archive. By algorithmically synthesizing and deconstructing these personal traces into a self-portrait, the work deploys technology against itself, functioning simultaneously as an ethical data citation, a formal technical critique, and an enduring act of self-reflection.

This video is part of the series ‘Nox’. Drawing from Rio Nakada’s lived experiences of complex PTSD, dissociation, and Alice in Wonderland Syndrome, the work translates internal psychological instability into an embodied sensory environment. Through fractured memories, shifting architectures, mirrored reflections, and visceral bodily distortions, the imagery renders an otherwise invisible, disorienting mental landscape spatial and tangible. Selected for the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, the project functions as an intimate bridge between isolation and communion, inviting the viewer into a briefly shared architecture of altered perception. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Knew the World in Fragments of Color’. Reflecting on the personal journey of migration from Venezuela to the United States, the project explores the dislocating experience of diaspora, cultural belonging, and the fractured nature of memory. Through meticulous staged compositions and handcrafted wearable constructions, the work harnesses heightened chromatic symbolism to reconstruct a displaced home, transforming personal nostalgia into a vivid, allegorical visual language.

Meet the international jury of Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, bringing together artists, photographers, editors, curators, and creative voices from different disciplines and backgrounds. Together with the Vogue and Condé Nast Committee, comprising more than 100 editorial and creative professionals from across our global brands, these jurors have brought their individual perspectives and sensibilities to the selection process. Their participation reflects something fundamental to PhotoVogue's philosophy: there is no single authority on what makes an image meaningful, no universal definition of beauty, and no one way of seeing the world. It is through the encounter of different perspectives that new possibilities emerge.

Born in Addis Ababa in 1974, Aïda graduated from Howard University with a degree in Communications, majoring in Film. Her photography is in major collections including MoMA, the Smithsonian, and the RISD Museum. She’s received numerous awards, including the EU Prize in Bamako, the CRAF Award, and the Royal Photographic Society Award. Aïda co-curated the Nobel Peace Prize exhibition in 2019 and was a commissioned artist in 2020. A Canon ambassador and founder of Addis Foto Fest and Africa Foto Fair, she also leads Africa Print House and advocates for health, the environment, and photography across Africa.

Alex Consani is a model and actress who was named 2024 Model of the Year at the Fashion Awards in London, becoming the first transgender woman to receive the award. A face of Gucci and YSL Beauty, she has graced the digital cover of American Vogue and made history as one of the first transgender women to walk the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Her acting credits include American Horror Story: 13 and A24’s upcoming film Peaked.

Curator, Founder & Artistic Director, Culture Art Society (CAS)

Awa Konaté is an independent curator, cultural strategist, and founder of Culture Art Society (CAS), a platform dedicated to research, exhibitions, and critical discourse on African and diasporic visual arts. Her practice draws on archival research, Black feminist pedagogies, and memory work, with a focus on interdisciplinary and lens-based practices by artists of African descent. She has collaborated with institutions including Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Serpentine Galleries, Raven Row, and the Barbican, and served on juries for Rencontres de Bamako and BlackStar Film Festival. Her writing has appeared in Third Text, Foam Magazine, and Phaidon, among other publications.

Elisa Medde is an Art Historian specializing in Photography and Visual Culture, focusing on image, communication, and power structures. She has chaired juries for awards like the Luma Rencontres Book Award and MAST Foundation Grant. Elisa collaborates with European universities including ECAL, HSLU, and UWE Bristol. She has curated photobooks and exhibitions, with writings in FlashArt, Time Magazine, Vogue Italia, and more. Editor-in-Chief of Foam Magazine (2012–2023), she won two Lucie Awards and received the 2023 Royal Photographic Society Award for outstanding achievement in Photography Publishing.

Fiona has over 20 years of picture editing experience across newspapers and is a curator, speaker on photojournalism, and mentor in the photography community. She was picture editor of The Guardian for ten years before becoming Head of Photography for Guardian News and Media Group. Fiona covered major historic events like 9/11, global conflicts, natural disasters, and refugee crises. She has judged awards including the Sony World Photography Awards, Taylor Wessing Portrait Prize, and chaired the 2024 World Press Photo Awards jury. Fiona also serves on the board of Stills Gallery, Edinburgh.

Florence Bourgeois has been Director of Paris Photo since 2015. With a background spanning fashion, luxury, and the art world, she previously held positions at Givenchy Parfums, Artcurial, and the Pavillon des Arts et du Design (PAD) in Paris and London. At Paris Photo, she has introduced initiatives including PRISMES, Emergence, and Elles x Paris Photo, developed in partnership with the French Ministry of Culture and Kering’s Women In Motion to increase the visibility and recognition of women artists. She has also overseen the fair’s international expansion in Los Angeles and New York and championed the acquisition of works by women artists through institutional partnerships. Actively involved in the photography ecosystem, she serves on numerous juries and commissions, supporting emerging talent and contemporary photography. In 2023, she was awarded the title of Officière des Arts et des Lettres by the French Minister of Culture.

Florentina Holzinger is an Austrian performance artist and choreographer whose work spans dance, theatre, and opera, exploring the limits of the body through extreme physicality and theatrical experimentation. Her practice challenges the boundaries between high culture and counterculture, spectacle and subversion, often incorporating body modification and a wide range of body-based disciplines. Her productions have received the Nestroy Award for TANZ (2020) and the Faust Award for Ophelia’s Got Talent (2023), and have been selected four times for Theatertreffen Berlin. Since 2021, she has been an associate artist at Volksbühne am Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz in Berlin. In 2026, she represents Austria at the 61st Venice Biennale.

Freelance Writer, Host, Brand Consultant, The Messy Truth Podcast

Gem Fletcher is a writer, consultant and podcaster. Her work has been published in Foam, Aperture, Dazed, Creative Review, 1000 Words and The British Journal of Photography. She also hosts The Messy Truth podcast, a series of candid conversations that unpack the future of visual culture and what it means to be a photographer today.

Ib Kamara is a Sierra Leone-born artist, stylist, and creative director known for his daring, interdisciplinary approach to fashion image-making. Raised in Gambia and educated at Central Saint Martins in London, he served as Editor-in-Chief of Dazed from 2021 to 2025 and Creative Director of Off-White from 2024 to 2026. His work spans editorial and commercial collaborations with artists including Beyoncé, Rihanna, Madonna, and Rosalía, and brands such as Chanel, Louis Vuitton, and Gucci. A contributor to international editions of Vogue, AnOther, and i-D, his work has been exhibited at Somerset House, Red Hook Labs, and the Victoria & Albert Museum. In 2021, he received the British Fashion Council’s Isabella Blow Award for Fashion Creator.

Stylist, Creative Consultant & Fashion Editor

Imruh Asha is a Paris-based stylist, creative consultant, and Fashion Director of Dazed, where he has been part of the team since 2021. Drawing on his Dutch-Caribbean roots and contemporary art, he brings a concept-driven and interdisciplinary approach to fashion image-making. Since his appointment as Fashion Director in 2022, he has pushed the boundaries of fashion imagery through ambitious collaborations, including projects that have broken three official Guinness World Records. In 2021, he presented Future Shock, his first sculpture exhibition, in collaboration with the Ere Foundation at Dover Street Market’s 3537 space.

Jennifer Pastore is an award-winning visual storyteller with more than two decades of experience shaping the imagery of leading magazines and cultural institutions. She is currently the Global Creative Director of Vanity Fair Magazine and previously held roles as the Visuals Director of Sotheby’s Magazine and the Executive Photography Director of WSJ. Magazine, where she commissioned photography, film, and illustration. Earlier in her career, she held roles at Harper’s Bazaar, Teen Vogue, and T: The New York Times Style Magazine. In 2022, she was awarded the Rome Prize in Design by the American Academy in Rome.

Photo Director, Artist & Curator. Former Director of Photography, The New York Times Magazine

Kathy Ryan was the longtime Director of Photography at The New York Times Magazine, where, over 39 years, she pioneered the integration of fine art photography and photojournalism, collaborating with leading photographers and championing new talent. She edited The New York Times Magazine Photographs (Aperture, 2011), which inspired an international touring exhibition, and is the author of Office Romance (Aperture, 2014), a collection of photographs made entirely on her iPhone. Since leaving the Times, she has focused on her own photographic practice, curating exhibitions, teaching at Yale, and speaking internationally. Her numerous accolades include the Royal Photographic Society Award for Outstanding Service to Photography (2012), the International Center of Photography's Spotlight Award (2024), and the Dr. Erich Salomon Prize (2025).

Kira Pollack is a creative director and photo editor pioneering visual storytelling through photography, technology, and digital media. A 2025 Walter Shorenstein Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School, she explores AI’s role in preserving visual history. Formerly Creative Director at Vanity Fair and Director of Photography at TIME, she led iconic projects including The 100 Most Influential Photographs and TIME’s first documentary film unit. Pollack’s work earned Emmy, Lucie, Webby, and National Magazine Awards. She has served as a juror for World Press Photo and Tribeca Film Festival and is based in New York City.

Founder & Creative Director, Be Good Studios

Lina Kutsovskaya is a creative director whose work bridges fashion, art, and advertising. She has led influential campaigns including #MyCalvins at Calvin Klein and creative collaborations with Virgil Abloh at Louis Vuitton. After beginning her career at Vogue, she held creative leadership roles at Nylon, Teen Vogue, Barneys New York, and Calvin Klein, before founding Be Good Studios, a creative agency working across campaigns, brand identity, publishing, and exhibition-making. From 2024 to 2026, she served as Art Director of Another Man, and in 2025 was appointed Contributing Creative Director of Vogue Japan. She is also the founder of Little Big Man, a gallery and publishing project based in Los Angeles.

Melissa Harris is Editor-at-Large at Aperture Foundation, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of Aperture magazine from 2002 to 2012, earning the publication a National Magazine Award for General Excellence. During her more than twenty years at Aperture, she edited over forty photography books and curated exhibitions internationally. Her curatorial projects include Mary Ellen Mark: Encounters (2023–2024), A Kind of Language at Fondazione Prada (2025), and a retrospective of Graciela Iturbide’s work at C/O Berlin (2026). She has taught at Yale, Columbia Journalism School, and New York University, where she has been part of the Tisch School of the Arts for twenty years. She is also Creative Director of Magnum Foundation’s ongoing US Dispatches / Time Capsule project.

Writer, Art Curator & Professor, New York University

Nicole R. Fleetwood is a writer, curator, and professor at New York University, as well as a MacArthur Fellow and elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. She is the author of Marking Time: Art in the Age of Mass Incarceration, which received the 2020 National Book Critics Circle Award, as well as On Racial Icons and Troubling Vision. Her curatorial projects have been presented at institutions including MoMA PS1, Aperture Foundation, the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, and the Brown Arts Institute. Her work has received support from leading cultural and research institutions, including the Mellon Foundation, Ford Foundation, and New York Public Library’s Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers.

Noelle Théard is a photographer, educator, and the US Head of Photography at The Guardian. Previously, she was Senior Photo Editor at The New Yorker, where she also produced Photo Booth, the magazine’s photography column. Her work focuses on social justice, community engagement, and the intersection of education and visual storytelling. She co-founded FotoKonbit, a nonprofit empowering Haitians to tell their own stories through photography, and has held roles at Magnum Foundation, Parsons, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Miami. She has also taught African Diaspora and Art History at Florida International University.

Member of the Board of Directors, Friends of Palais de Tokyo

Olivia Anani is a Paris-based curator, writer, and art market expert with a background in Asian Studies and Contemporary Art. She has worked at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips, contributing to the sale of major masters and the reevaluation of African artists. Olivia serves on the Board of Friends of Palais de Tokyo and leads its Young Patrons initiative. She supports institutions like the Louvre and is involved in developing a new cultural institution in Benin. Anani has contributed to major monographs and was named among France’s 100 Most Influential Women in Culture in 2021.

Willow Defebaugh is the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Atmos, an award-winning climate and culture magazine that seeks to re-enchant people with our shared humanity and the Earth. She is the author of The Overview, a deep ecology newsletter and book, and host of The Nature Of, a podcast from Atmos. She is a lifelong student of nature and graduated with a degree in creative writing from the University of Michigan. Her work has been featured in Vogue, Harper's Bazaar, Teen Vogue, V Magazine, Interview, i-D, BBC, The Guardian, Them, New York Magazine, and more. She lives in Brooklyn on unceded Lenape territory.

#6599. BA's Best Lasagna

This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells.

The secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture.

One step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad.

Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles?

No—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted.

Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella?

This is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna.

What’s the best way to split up the work?

Make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day.

Saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

Preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

Add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

Using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

Do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

Melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

Note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

If parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

Lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

Do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

Editor’s note: This recipe first appeared in our February 2018 issue as part of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. #6598. This $20 Gadget Is My Grandpa’s Secret To Making Big-Batch Potatoes For The Holidays

It looks a little ridiculous, but I can’t stop watching it work.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Growing up, there was one thing I could always count on: If I expressed even a hint of interest in something my grandpa had, I’d have my very own on my doorstep the minute I returned home... and so would every other member of our family. That’s how we became a family full of Rotatos.

If you don’t know what a Rotato is, allow me to introduce you. This rather bare-bones machine will seamlessly peel your potatoes (and other fruits and veggies, too) in just seconds—and the entertainment value is off the charts.

One day while I was visiting my grandparents, I watched my grandfather use his Rotato to peel enough potatoes for a large batch of latkes, then fry up all the peels. His giant batches allowed him to freeze his latkes and enjoy them for months on end. But why spend time peeling all those potatoes yourself when you could whip out a handy gadget that does it all for you?

The Rotato is a mesmerizing device. Sure, it’s a single-use kitchen product, but I could literally watch this baby peel things for hours. Since I first expressed my awe and received one of my very own (along with my parents, sister, and cousins), I’ve tried the Rotato on all kinds of produce.

Mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up new recipes.

Since discovering the magic of the Rotato, I’ve used it to make mashed potatoes for Friendsgiving, fruit salad, and much more. Sure, it doesn’t get used consistently year-round, but when you’re cooking for a crew, it’s the handiest thing in the kitchen.

#6596. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#6595. 21 Easy Thanksgiving Appetizers That Make Hosting A Breeze

Thanksgiving asks a lot of us (and our ovens!). From making the turkey to all of the casseroles and sides, don’t even get me started on dessert. You’ve got a lot on your plate, so we’re trying to make the big turkey day a little easier. Appetizers are my favorite part of the meal: little bites that pack so much flavor and fun into the start of the big feast, so you’ve gotta make them count. We’ve got some clever, simple shortcuts to help you whip up appetizers that will impress your guests without adding to your stress.

Whether you’re looking for quick and easy last-minute options or want something more elaborate, we’ve got something on this list for you. Need more Thanksgiving hosting ideas? Check out our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes and Thanksgiving cocktails!

Sweet and savory with a kick of heat, these pumpkin, Brie, and hot honey bites are the perfect fall appetizer to serve during the holidays. The honey provides the perfect balance for the sweetness of the pumpkin and the savory, melty Brie. Add a bit of fresh thyme and some roasted pecans, and you’ve got yourself a certified crowd-pleaser.

There is nothing better than a soft, homemade dinner roll. These rolls use sweet potatoes to make them even softer and fluffier, similar to our classic potato rolls. These would be a fun alternative to biscuits or Parker House rolls at Thanksgiving or another big family meal.

Having multiple Thanksgivings this year? Want to transform your leftovers from one into something incredible for the next? Look no further than this stuffed bread ring—it's gorgeous and super easy, thanks to store-bought crescent roll dough.

With all of the elements of stuffing plus the added flaky and butter benefits of biscuits, this pull-apart stuffing bread just might start a tug-of-war situation at your table when you grab for a slice.

It’s a tail as old as time: It’s right before Thanksgiving dinner, and your guests don’t want a full meal but are feeling a little peckish. Try a bird of a different feather this year, and serve this festive and impressive fruit and cheese display as the centerpiece of your holiday app table.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. Preparing these potato skins is simple; all you need for this recipe are Thanksgiving leftovers and a few additional pantry staples: potatoes and cheddar cheese.

It’s hard to find a party appetizer that’s more beloved than a cheese log—or its alternate form, the cheese ball. Here, dried sweetened cranberries, walnuts, and fresh thyme conjure a holiday feeling, while a little honey complements the sweet-tart fruit.

These are a fan favorite every fall. They always disappear within minutes, probably because the combo of salty, creamy brie, sweet-tart cranberry sauce, and crunchy pecans is PERFECT.

Fall desserts may get all the attention once autumn comes around, but I'm here to say that seasonal appetizers deserve their share of the spotlight—especially these adorable pizza-stuffed pumpkins. Stuffed with creamy ricotta, these biscuit-based bites are baked to golden perfection before being brushed with a flavor-packed garlic butter.

Just like our famous cranberry brie bites, these little guys are hard to put down! They're the perfect amount of sweet and savory, so you can serve them before or after the big meal.

Sausage Stuffing Bites With Cranberry Sauce

Stuffing, inside the turkey or out, is a Thanksgiving staple. The only thing better? MORE. STUFFING. Enter this bite-sized, stuffing-centered appetizer with a tangy, three-ingredient dipping sauce (just cranberry sauce, honey, and Dijon).

Even if you're not serving turkey this Thanksgiving doesn't mean you can't get in on the theme. Enter: this adorable cheeseball. We used carrots, pecans, pretzels, and bell peppers to create the iconic look, but feel free to substitute them with different ingredients for what you have on hand. Serve it with crackers and use the decorations as dippers too!

These sweet potato bites have a crunchy, herbaceous crust, with a sweet, silky inside that, when topped with a light drizzle of honey, will have you craving them again and again. Once you bite through the crust, the sweet potato mixes with that melted, nutty Gruyère for a dream flavor combination that works SO well.

Cranberry brie bites are by far one of our favorite appetizers for the holidays, but jalapeño poppers also have place in our hearts too... So why not combine them? The spice of the jalapeño goes so well with the tart cranberries.

To make these, we stuff baby bella mushrooms with garlicky, herby breadcrumbs and plenty of cheese. Stuff them ahead of time and bake them off when you're ready for the most Thanksgiving-friendly appetizer ever.

Pull-apart bread reaches a whole new level, thanks to brie and cranberry sauce. Use your favorite homemade sauce recipes, but store-bought works too if you're short for time.

Little puff pastry squares get topped with caramelized onions and a little crumbled goat cheese for an easy appetizer that always wows. The final step is a light drizzle of honey for that salty sweet combination everyone will love.

If you’re a fan of our cranberry brie bites, we’ve got news for you: There’s a new app in town, and it’s inspired by another fan fave, baked feta pasta. These features the flavors you know and love, all nestled into bite-sized cups of golden crescent roll dough.

There's something very classic about the crescent roll dough flavor, so we tend to gravitate toward it, but puff pastry or even biscuit dough should both work here, too.

Think this sounds like a strange combo? You've gotta trust us on this one. If the aroma of toasted puff pastry, roasted apples, and nutty cheddar cheese doesn’t wake up your spirit… we're not sure what will.

#6593. This Jewelry Designer Bride Created Her Own Vintage-Inspired Dress for Her Polish Countryside Wedding

When the Polish jewelry designer Natalia Kopiszka was planning her August 2026 wedding to actor Aleksander “Olek” Kaleta, she found herself at a bridal fashion crossroads, stuck between two stylistic pillars of her own brand: vintage and modern.

First, the Warsaw-based designer of Kopi traveled to Paris to shop for a vintage wedding dress, but returned home empty-handed. “I didn’t find anything that I liked, so I thought: I will design my own wedding dress,” Natalia says.

For the body of her ceremony dress, she ordered fabric—silk taffeta—from Etsy. “I was on a mission to find the absolute dream silk fabric,” she says. “I started by checking out local fabric shops and silk wholesalers, but I just couldn't find the right silk taffeta with that delicate, subtle sheen anywhere.” She searched online and stumbled upon a listing from a New York-based seller, which she ordered on the spot. Luckily, “it turned out to be even more breathtaking in person than in the photos,” she says.

Then, on a weekend trip to Amsterdam with a friend, she wandered into a vintage store where she found antique lace, which she used for the bodice detailing. “The lace is truly unique because it dates back to the early 20th century, and I only had a tiny piece of it—which happened to be just enough to trim the bodice,” Natalia says. “It was such a special way to check off the ‘something old’ tradition.” She sketched the dress, then shared her designs with a dressmaker who sewed it, making her vintage-modern dream a reality.

Natalia and Olek first met in February 2021 at a house party in Warsaw. “For me, it was love at first sight,” Natalia recalls. “A friend of mine who lived in the apartment below me threw a get-together, and her roommate happened to be friends with Olek. As soon as he walked in, we instantly locked eyes. I’m pretty sure he was the one who came over and started the conversation first,” she adds. “It also turned out that Olek lived directly across the street from my apartment, so we used to wave at each other from our windows. Ever since that night, we started seeing each other almost every single day.”

After a year, they moved in together in Warsaw. In 2024, Olek proposed to Natalia during a trip to Italy, in the coastal town of Polignano a Mare. “It was a warm, romantic evening with a huge moon, and surprisingly, I didn't see it coming at all,” Natalia says. “It turned out to be such a sweet, funny moment because neither of us could stop laughing.”

On August 8, 2026, the couple held their wedding at Pałac Pstrokonie, a historic 19th-century palace in a small village outside of Warsaw. They worked with the wedding planner Kasia Fastyn, who brought Natalia’s vision—a romantic, whimsical wonderland of sorts—to life, pairing them with the event studio MyBigDay, who designed the florals and draped their dancing tent in pink fabric.

As a jewelry and accessories designer, Natalia zeroed in on all the details of her wedding looks from the beginning. She knew she didn’t want a traditional floral bouquet, for example, so she opted for a small silk bag in the shape of a bouquet from the New York-based designer Camille Albertine, after finding her work on Instagram. Albertine custom-made Natalia’s bouquet purse in the same fabric as her dress. “Everyone was so surprised that I didn’t have a typical bouquet,” Natalia says. “It’s versatile enough that I can wear it with everyday outfits. It’s going to stay with me for a long time, and I’ll even be able to pass it down through generations.”

For her reception look, the bride changed into a dress by the Polish designer Magda Butrym, pairing it with an unexpected accessory: a crochet veil cap that her sister made. “It was a really simple dress, also silk, but I put something really crazy on my head,” Natalia says.

Natalia incorporated her own jewelry into the crochet cap-like veil, which was bedazzled with charms and pendants. “They are specially made charms with little lobster clasps so you can clip them onto the crochet work however you like. They’re gold-plated and feature Swarovski crystals,” Natalia says. (Charms are a signature of Natalia’s brand, she explains, so it was only fitting to work them into her bridal looks.) Her love of historical pieces, particularly from the Victorian era, inspired the final design, which included blue stones for her “something blue.” A look inspired by it is now for sale as part of Kopi’s “I Do” bridal line.

The bride also made Olek a pocket square with the same vintage lace as her dress, so they were matching (and so he had “something old” as well). They completed their looks with wedding bands that Natalia designed. “Mine has a retro feel, crafted in gold and set with 12 small diamonds,” she says of the rings. “Olek went for a classic look—a simple, wide gold band with my nickname engraved on the inside.” Reflecting on the wedding months later, Natalia says: “Everything was perfect.”

It was a far cry, fashion-wise, from the past few weeks in Catherine’s diary. A visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with the Prince of Wales saw her inadvertently twinning with Bridgerton’s Simone Ashley in Mumbai, and wearing a hand-embroidered anarkali by New Delhi designer Mahima Mahajan, paired with jewels from Queen Elizabeth II’s collection.

Kate wearing the same jacket three years ago in South Wales.

According to fashion folklore, when Barbour offered to replace the monarch’s well-worn Beaufort style, she chose to keep the original for another 25 years. Like her husband’s grandmother before her, given the opportunity, Kate always looks happy to swap occasionwear for clothes better suited to navigating muddy fields—like waterproofs and walking boots. Her check-lined jacket has been in her wardrobe since at least 2023, when she wore it on a visit to South Wales with her husband.

At the Hugo Burge Foundation in Greenlaw, Scotland.

Kate Middleton is famously passionate about nature, and the sporty royal completed the grueling Three Peaks Challenge over the summer after recovering following treatment for cancer. Over the weekend, the palace released an emotional trailer for Heal, a deeply personal documentary in which Catherine reflects on her cancer diagnosis and recovery.

#6590. Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor

With a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking
